Nobody can be forced to pay a tax whose proceeds are set aside to promote or maintain a particular religion or denomination.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The bar is on a tax, not a fee. A charge for a service actually rendered, such as regulating a pilgrimage or running a shrine, is a fee and is allowed.

Most State control of religious endowments rests on that difference.

sections.t: Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions
sections.b: (1) No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds. (2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to an educational institution which is administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution. (3) No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction that may be imparted in such institution or to attend any religious worship that may be conducted in such institution or in any premises attached thereto unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto.
sections.cm:
A school wholly maintained out of State funds may give no religious instruction at all. The exception is a school the State runs under an endowment or trust that requires such instruction.

In a school the State recognises or aids, nobody may be made to attend religious instruction or worship without consent.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The rule changes with the funding. A school paid for wholly by the State faces a total ban. An aided or recognised school must only let pupils opt out.

Nothing here bans teaching about religions. What is regulated is instruction in a faith.

sections.t: Protection of interests of minorities
sections.b: (1) Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same. (2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them.
sections.cm:
Any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it.

Separately, no citizen may be refused admission to an educational institution run or aided by the State on grounds only of religion, race, caste or language.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Clause (1) protects "any section of citizens", not only minorities. So a majority community with a distinct culture is covered too.

Clause (2) once blocked caste quotas. In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Court struck down a caste-based quota in Madras medical colleges under clause (2). Parliament replied with the First Amendment, which added Article 15(4) to allow such quotas.

sections.t: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
sections.b: (1) All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice. 1[(1A) In making any law providing for the compulsory acquisition of any property of an educational institution established and administered by a minority, referred to in clause (1), the State shall ensure that the amount fixed by or determined under such law for the acquisition of such property is such as would not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under that clause.] (2) The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language. 2* * * *
sections.cm:
All minorities, religious or linguistic, may set up and run educational institutions of their choice.

The State may not discriminate against a minority institution when giving aid. If the State acquires the institution's property, the amount it pays must not defeat the right.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The right is unusually strong. In T.M.A. Pai (2002) an eleven-judge bench held that the State may set standards of teaching, qualifications and syllabus. But the State may not take over the running of the institution.

The right also belongs only to minorities. Article 15(5), which allows reservation in private institutions, does not apply to minority institutions. Pramati (2014) held that the Right to Education Act does not apply to them either. So minority status is worth a great deal, and it is often fought over in court.

cl.name: T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
cl.facts: Private and minority professional colleges challenged State control over admissions and fees. An eleven-judge bench was assembled to settle the rights of private and minority institutions once and for all.
cl.held: Minority status is determined State-wise, not nationally. Private unaided institutions have autonomy over admission and fees, subject to the State's power to ensure merit, transparency and no profiteering. Aided institutions accept more regulation.
cl.why: The governing statement on private and minority education. Islamic Academy and P.A. Inamdar are attempts to work out what it meant in practice.

cl.name: Aligarh Muslim University v. Naresh Agarwal
cl.facts: Whether AMU is a minority institution under Article 30 had been contested since Azeez Basha (1968), which held that a university created by statute cannot be a minority institution.
cl.held: By 4–3, Azeez Basha was overruled. An institution does not lose minority character merely because it was incorporated by statute; what matters is who founded it and for whose benefit. The question of AMU's own status was sent to a regular bench applying this test.
cl.why: It reopened minority status for institutions created by law, with consequences well beyond AMU.

sections.t: Compulsory acquisition of property
sections.b: Omitted.
sections.cm:
Article 31 was the old fundamental right to property. Nobody could be deprived of property except by authority of law, and compulsory acquisition required compensation.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 44th Amendment repealed the article in 1978, after nearly thirty years of conflict between land reform and the courts.

Property is now protected only by Article 300A, which is a constitutional right, not a fundamental one. So a person cannot go to the Supreme Court under Article 32 to enforce it.

sections.t: Saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc
sections.b:
5[(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law providing for— (a) the acquisition by the State of any estate or of any rights therein or the extinguishment or modification of any such rights; or (b) the taking over of the management of any property by the State for a limited period either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of the property; or (c) the amalgamation of two or more corporations either in the public interest or in order to secure the proper management of any of the corporations; or (d) the extinguishment or modification of any rights of managing agents, secretaries and treasurers, managing directors, directors or managers of corporations, or of any voting rights of shareholders thereof; or (2) In this article,— 3[(a) the expression “estate” shall, in relation to any local area, have the same meaning as that expression or its local equivalent has in the existing law relating to land tenures in force in that area and shall also include— (i) any jagir, inam or muafi or other similar grant and in the States of 4[Tamil Nadu] and Kerala, any janmam right; (ii) any land held under ryotwari settlement; (iii) any land held or let for purposes of agriculture or for purposes ancillary thereto, including waste land, forest land, land for pasture or sites of buildings and other structures occupied by cultivators of land, agricultural labourers and village artisans;] article 19 or article 31" "Madras" (b) the expression “rights”, in relation to an estate, shall include any rights vesting in a proprietor, sub-proprietor, under-proprietor, tenure-holder, 1[raiyat, under-raiyat] or other intermediary and any rights or privileges in respect of land revenue.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 4 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). 3. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 3 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). 4. Ins. by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s. 4, (with retrospective effect). 5. Subs. by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, s. 3, for cl. (1) (with 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 7, for "article 14, 2. Ins. by the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, s. 2(i) (w.e.f. 20-6-1964). 3. Subs. by s.2(ii), ibid., for sub-clause (a) (with retrospective effect). 4. Subs. by the Madras State (Alteration of Name) Act, 1968 (53 of 1968), s. 4, for 2. Sub-heading "Right to Property" omitted by s. 5, ibid. (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). retrospective effect). (e) the extinguishment or modification of any rights accruing by virtue of any agreement, lease or licence for the purpose of searching for, or winning, any mineral or mineral oil, or the premature termination or cancellation of any such agreement, lease or licence, shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by 1[article 14 or article 19]: Provided that where such law is a law made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent:] 2[Provided further that where any law makes any provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force or any building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to the acquisition of such land, building or structure, provides for payment of compensation at a rate which shall not be less than the market value thereof.]]
sections.cm:
Article 31A protects certain kinds of law from challenge under Articles 14 and 19. They are laws acquiring estates, taking over the management of property, merging companies, changing the rights of directors, shareholders or managing agents, and changing mining leases.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 31A survives even though Article 31 itself is gone.

Two provisos matter. A State law of this kind needs the President's assent. And land within the ceiling limit that the owner personally cultivates cannot be acquired without compensation at market value.

sections.t: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
sections.b: Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in article 31A, none of the Acts and Regulations specified in the Ninth Schedule nor any of the provisions thereof shall be deemed to be void, or ever to have become void, on the ground that such Act, Regulation or provision is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by, any provisions of this Part, and notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of any court or Tribunal to the contrary, each of the said Acts and Regulations shall, subject to the power of any competent Legislature to repeal or amend it, continue in force.]
sections.cm:
A law placed in the Ninth Schedule cannot be struck down for breaching a fundamental right. The protection is retrospective, so even a law a court has already struck down revives.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The First Amendment (1951) created the Ninth Schedule to shield land-reform laws from landlords' challenges. The Schedule began with 13 laws and now holds over 280, many of them unrelated to land.

I.R. Coelho (2007) limited the shield. A law added after 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda, can still be struck down if it damages the basic structure.

cl.name: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
cl.facts: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda were challenged. Article 31B says a Ninth Schedule law cannot be questioned for violating fundamental rights.
cl.held: Any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 — the date of Kesavananda — is open to challenge if it damages the basic structure, tested by the effect the law has on Part III rights, not merely its form.
cl.why: It ended the Ninth Schedule as an absolute shield. Around 284 entries sit there; those added after 1973 are now all vulnerable.

cl.name: Waman Rao v. Union of India
cl.facts: Maharashtra agricultural land-ceiling laws placed in the Ninth Schedule were challenged after Kesavananda.
cl.held: Amendments made before 24 April 1973 are immune; those made after that date are open to basic-structure review. Articles 31A and 31C, as they stood before the 42nd Amendment, were upheld.
cl.why: It fixed the Kesavananda date as the constitutional dividing line, which Coelho then applied to the Ninth Schedule.

sections.t: Saving of laws giving effect to certain directive principles
sections.b: Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing 4[all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV] shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by 5[article 14 or article 19;] 6[and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy]: Provided that where such law is made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent.]
sections.cm:
A law made to carry out Article 39(b) or (c) cannot be challenged under Article 14 or Article 19. The two clauses deal with sharing the community's material resources and preventing concentration of wealth.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 25th Amendment (1971) added the article. Its original version also said no court could ask whether a law really served those principles. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) struck that sentence down.

In 1976 the 42nd Amendment extended the protection to laws for any directive principle. Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the extension, holding that the balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure. So only the narrow version survives.

cl.name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
cl.facts: A textile mill was nationalised. The challenge grew into an attack on two clauses the 42nd Amendment had inserted — Article 368(4) and (5), which purported to put amendments beyond judicial review and declare the amending power unlimited.
cl.held: Both clauses struck down: limited amending power is itself part of the basic structure, and a power to destroy cannot be conferred on the amending body. The 42nd Amendment's widening of Article 31C to all directive principles was also struck down, since the balance between Parts III and IV is a basic feature.
cl.why: It confirmed that Parliament cannot amend away judicial review of amendments, and restored Article 31C to its pre-1976 shape.

sections.t: Saving of laws in respect of anti-national activities
sections.b:
Omitted.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, s. 3 (with retrospective effect). 2. Ins. by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s. 5 (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). 3. Ins. by the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 (w.e.f. 20-4-1972). 4. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 4, for “the principles 5. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 8, for “article 14, article 6. The words in italics struck down by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of 7. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 5 (w.e.f. 03-01-1977).]
sections.cm:
Article 31D once protected laws against "anti-national activities" from challenge under the fundamental rights.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment inserted it during the Emergency, and the 43rd repealed it in 1977. The repeal is one of the clearest signs of how quickly the Emergency changes were reversed.

sections.t: Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part
sections.b: (1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed. (2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part. (3) Without prejudice to the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by clauses (1) and (2), Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under clause (2). (4) The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution.
sections.cm:
Article 32 gives a person the right to go straight to the Supreme Court when a fundamental right is violated. The right to go to the Court is itself a fundamental right.

The Court can issue five writs to enforce the rights: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 32 covers fundamental rights and nothing else. A person whose ordinary legal right is broken cannot come here. The High Courts under Article 226 have wider power, because they may issue the same writs "for any other purpose" as well.

But the Court has widened who may use Article 32. Since the late 1970s, any public-spirited person may move the Court for people who cannot, which is public interest litigation. So Article 32 is narrow in what it covers, but wide in who may use it.

Practitioner Note:
During the 1975 Emergency, the right to move any court to enforce Article 21 was suspended. ADM Jabalpur (1976) upheld the suspension, and Puttaswamy (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur.

cl.name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
cl.facts: Lawyers challenged the government's refusal to confirm additional judges and the transfer of a Chief Justice, and had to establish that they had standing to bring the case at all.
cl.held: Any member of the public acting bona fide may move the Court for a legal wrong suffered by a person or class unable to approach it themselves. On the merits, 'consultation' with the Chief Justice did not mean concurrence — the executive had primacy in judicial appointments.
cl.why: It opened the door to public interest litigation in India. Its holding on appointments was reversed by the Second Judges Case in 1993.

cl.name: Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
cl.facts: The Court was asked whether it could reconsider a final judgment after a review petition had already been dismissed.
cl.held: Yes, in rare cases, through a newly created 'curative petition' — where there was a violation of natural justice or the judge did not disclose a conflict of interest. It must be certified by a senior advocate and is normally decided in chambers.
cl.why: The last remedy in the Indian legal system, created by the Court out of Article 142 rather than by any statute.

sections.t: Constitutional validity of State laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 32
sections.b: Omitted.
sections.cm:
Article 32A once barred the Supreme Court from deciding whether a State law was constitutional in a case brought under Article 32.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment inserted it, and the 43rd repealed it in 1977.

sections.t: Power of Parliament to modify the rights conferred by this Part in their application to Forces, etc
sections.b:
Parliament may, by law, determine to what extent any of the rights conferred by this Part shall, in their application to,— (a) the members of the Armed Forces; or (b) the members of the Forces charged with the maintenance of public order; or (c) persons employed in any bureau or other organisation established by the State for purposes of intelligence or counter intelligence; or (d) person employed in, or in connection with, the telecommunication systems set up for the purposes of any Force, bureau or organisation referred to in clauses (a) to (c), be restricted or abrogated so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 6 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977). 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Fiftieth Amendment) Act, 1984, s. 2, for art. 33]
sections.cm:
Parliament may restrict or take away the fundamental rights of the armed forces, the police, paramilitary forces and intelligence services, so that they do their duty and keep discipline. The power also covers people in telecommunication systems set up for these forces.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Only Parliament may do this, not a State legislature. And Parliament must act by a law, not by an executive order. So a State cannot restrict the rights of even its own police.

The reason is discipline. The Army Act, the Navy Act and the Air Force Act limit the speech, association and assembly of service personnel. So members of the armed forces cannot form trade unions.

sections.t: Restriction on rights conferred by this Part while martial law is in force in any area
sections.b: Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, Parliament may by law indemnify any person in the service of the Union or of a State or any other person in respect of any act done by him in connection with the maintenance or restoration of order in any area within the territory of India where martial law was in force or validate any sentence passed, punishment inflicted, forfeiture ordered or other act done under martial law in such area.
sections.cm:
Where martial law has been in force, Parliament may by law protect anyone from liability for acts done to keep or restore order there. Parliament may also validate sentences and punishments passed under martial law.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Constitution never defines martial law, and Parliament has never passed such an Act.

Martial law is not the same as an emergency under Part XVIII. Martial law displaces the ordinary courts in an area. An emergency does not.

sections.t: Legislation to give effect to the provisions of this Part
sections.b: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,— (a) Parliament shall have, and the Legislature of a State shall not have, power to make laws— (i) with respect to any of the matters which under clause (3) of article 16, clause (3) of article 32, article 33 and article 34 may be provided for by law made by Parliament; and (ii) for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under this Part, and Parliament shall, as soon as may be after the commencement of this Constitution, make laws for prescribing punishment for the acts referred to in sub-clause (ii); (b) any law in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution in the territory of India with respect to any of the matters referred to in sub-clause (i) of clause (a) or providing for punishment for any act referred to in sub-clause (ii) of that clause shall, subject to the terms thereof and to any adaptations and modifications that may be made therein under article 372, continue in force until altered or repealed or amended by Parliament. Explanation.—In this article, the expression "law in force'' has the same meaning as in article 372.
sections.cm:
Only Parliament may make laws under Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34. Only Parliament may set the punishment for the acts that Articles 17 and 23 make offences. A State legislature can do neither.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 35 overrides the usual split of law-making power in the Seventh Schedule. On these matters a State legislature has no power, even where the subject would otherwise belong to it.

The reason is uniformity. The content of these fundamental rights, and the punishment for breaking them, must not change from State to State.

sections.t: Definition
sections.b: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, “the State” has the same meaning as in Part III.
sections.cm:
In Part IV, "the State" means the same as in Article 12. The term covers the governments, the legislatures, and all local and other authorities.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Part IV borrows the definition from Part III. So the directive principles are addressed to exactly the same bodies that the fundamental rights bind.

But the result is weaker here. A citizen can go to court over a breach of Part III, but not over a breach of Part IV.

sections.t: Application of the principles contained in this Part
sections.b: The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
sections.cm:
No court can enforce the directive principles. But the principles are fundamental to governing the country, and the State has a duty to apply them in making laws.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 37 is the reason Part IV reads like a set of goals, not a list of rights.

But "not enforceable" does not mean "irrelevant". Courts use the directive principles to give content to fundamental rights, to judge whether a restriction is reasonable, and to uphold laws that put the principles into effect. The right to a clean environment, for example, came from reading Article 48A into Article 21.

cl.name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
cl.facts: The 42nd Amendment had widened Article 31C so that a law made to give effect to ANY directive principle was immune from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
cl.held: Struck down. Parts III and IV together form the core of the Constitution, and 'to give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution'. That balance is itself a basic feature.
cl.why: The definitive statement of the relationship between fundamental rights and directive principles — neither subordinate, both to be read harmoniously.

sections.t: State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people
sections.b: 1[(1)] The State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life. 2[(2) The State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations.]
sections.cm:
The State shall work for a social order in which social, economic and political justice shapes every national institution. The State shall also try to reduce inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The second rule, on reducing inequality, came with the 44th Amendment in 1978. The same amendment removed the right to property from Part III.

sections.t: Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State
sections.b:
The State shall, in particular, direct its policy towards securing— (a) that the citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood; (b) that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good; (c) that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment; (d) that there is equal pay for equal work for both men and women; (e) that the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused and that citizens are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength; 1978, s. 9 1[(f) that children are given opportunities and facilities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity and that childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Art. 38 renumbered as cl. (1) by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2. Ins. by s. 9, ibid. (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).]
sections.cm:
Article 39 gives the State six economic goals.

Everyone should have an adequate livelihood. The community's material resources should serve the common good. Wealth should not pile up in a few hands. Men and women should get equal pay for equal work. Workers and children should not be abused. And children should be able to grow up in freedom and dignity.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Clauses (b) and (c) have extra armour. A law made to carry them out is protected by Article 31C, so the law cannot be struck down for breaching Articles 14 or 19.

So the meaning of "material resources of the community" decides how far the State can reach into private property. In Property Owners' Association (2024), nine judges held that not every privately owned resource counts.

cl.name: Property Owners' Association v. State of Maharashtra
cl.facts: A Maharashtra law let a State board take over dilapidated Mumbai buildings. The question was whether privately owned property counts as 'material resources of the community' under Article 39(b), which would attract Article 31C's protection.
cl.held: By 8–1, not every privately owned resource is a material resource of the community. Whether a particular resource qualifies depends on its nature, scarcity, and the consequences of concentrating it in private hands. The broad view taken in Ranganatha Reddy and Sanjeev Coke was disapproved.
cl.why: It narrowed a doctrine that, read widely, would have allowed almost any private property to be redistributed under cover of Article 39(b).

sections.t: Equal justice and free legal aid
sections.b: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice, on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal aid, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.]
sections.cm:
The State shall make sure the legal system delivers justice on equal terms. The State shall provide free legal aid, so that no citizen is denied justice because of poverty or any other disability.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 39A. Few directive principles have become so real.

In Hussainara Khatoon (1979) the Court held that free legal aid is part of a fair procedure under Article 21. The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 then gave the right its machinery, through national, State and District authorities and Lok Adalats.

sections.t: Organisation of village panchayats
sections.b: The State shall take steps to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to enable them to function as units of self-government.
sections.cm:
The State shall organise village panchayats and give them the powers they need to work as units of self-government.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Constituent Assembly was divided on village government. Gandhi wanted village republics. Ambedkar saw the village as a sink of localism, ignorance and narrow-mindedness. So the principle went into Part IV, where no court could enforce it.

For over forty years, panchayats depended on the goodwill of each State. The 73rd Amendment (1992) then added Part IX, which made panchayats a constitutional requirement.

sections.t: Right to work, to education and to public assistance in certain cases
sections.b: The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of undeserved want.
sections.cm:
Within the limits of its economic capacity, the State shall provide for the right to work, to education, and to public help in unemployment, old age, sickness and disability.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The words "within the limits of its economic capacity and development" make Article 41 a goal, not an entitlement.

sections.t: Provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief
sections.b: The State shall make provision for securing just and humane conditions of work and for maternity relief.
sections.cm:
The State shall provide for just and humane conditions of work, and for maternity relief.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 42 is the basis of the Maternity Benefit Act and much other law protecting workers. Courts have also used it to read dignity at work into Article 21.

sections.t: Living wage, etc., for workers
sections.b: The State shall endeavour to secure, by suitable legislation or economic organisation or in any other way, to all workers, agricultural, industrial or otherwise, work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.
sections.cm:
The State shall try to secure for all workers a living wage, decent working conditions, a decent standard of life, and full use of leisure. The State shall also promote cottage industries in rural areas.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A living wage is a higher standard than a minimum wage. No law has ever set a living wage as such.

sections.t: Participation of workers in management of industries
sections.b:
The State shall take steps, by suitable legislation or in any other way, to secure the participation of workers in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in any industry.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 7, for cl. (f) 2. Ins. by s. 8, ibid. (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). 3. Ins. by s. 9, ibid. (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).]
sections.cm:
The State shall take steps to give workers a share in the management of industries.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment added the article. Almost no legislation has followed it.

sections.t: Promotion of co-operative societies
sections.b: The State shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.]
sections.cm:
The State shall promote co-operative societies that are formed voluntarily, work independently, are controlled democratically and are managed professionally.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 97th Amendment (2011) added Article 43B, added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c), and inserted a new Part IXB.

But co-operatives are a State subject, and Part IXB never got the ratification of half the States that Article 368 requires. In Rajendra N. Shah (2021) the Court struck Part IXB down for co-operatives within a State. Article 43B and the change to Article 19(1)(c) survive.

sections.t: Uniform civil code for the citizens
sections.b: The State shall endeavour to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.
sections.cm:
The State shall try to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens throughout India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A civil code covers marriage, divorce, maintenance, inheritance, adoption and succession. India already has one criminal law for everyone. But these personal matters are governed by separate laws for Hindus, Muslims, Christians and Parsis.

Article 44 cannot be enforced, so no court can order a uniform code into existence. In Shah Bano (1985) and Sarla Mudgal (1995) the Court urged Parliament to act, and Parliament did not. So a uniform code exists only where a legislature has made one, as Uttarakhand did in 2024, or where one was inherited, as in Goa.

cl.name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
cl.facts: A 62-year-old divorced Muslim woman claimed maintenance under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Her husband argued that under Muslim personal law his obligation ended after the iddat period.
cl.held: Section 125 is a secular provision that applies to everyone regardless of religion, so she was entitled to maintenance. The Court also urged Parliament to enact a uniform civil code under Article 44.
cl.why: The political reaction produced the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which sought to reverse it — and the Court then read that Act, in Danial Latifi (2001), as still requiring a fair provision for life.

cl.name: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India
cl.facts: Hindu husbands converted to Islam in order to marry a second time without dissolving the first marriage.
cl.held: A Hindu marriage can be dissolved only under the Hindu Marriage Act. Conversion does not automatically end it, so the second marriage is void and the husband is liable for bigamy under Section 494 IPC.
cl.why: It closed a well-used loophole, and repeated the call for a uniform civil code that Article 44 leaves unenforceable.

sections.t: Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years
sections.b: The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.]
sections.cm:
The State shall provide early childhood care and education for all children until they turn six.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 45 used to say something else. Until 2002 it promised free and compulsory education for all children up to fourteen, within ten years of 1950. The deadline was missed by more than forty years.

The 86th Amendment (2002) moved the promise for ages six to fourteen into Article 21A, as an enforceable fundamental right. Only children under six were left in Article 45, where the promise still cannot be enforced.

sections.t: Promotion of educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections
sections.b: The State shall promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, and shall protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.
sections.cm:
The State shall take special care to promote the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, especially the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The State shall also protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 46 is the policy reason most often given for reservation. Courts cite it, alongside Articles 15(4) and 16(4), to show that reservation and welfare schemes serve a goal the Constitution sets.

But Article 46 creates no quota itself. The power to reserve comes from other articles. Article 46 supplies only the reason.

sections.t: Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living and to improve public health
sections.b: The State shall regard the raising of the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people and the improvement of public health as among its primary duties and, in particular, the State shall endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption except for medicinal purposes of intoxicating drinks and of drugs which are injurious to health.
sections.cm:
The State shall raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living, and improve public health. The State shall also try to bring about prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs, except for medical use.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
State bans on liquor, such as Bihar's in 2016, rest on the prohibition clause.

sections.t: Organisation of agriculture and animal husbandry
sections.b: The State shall endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and shall, in particular, take steps for preserving and improving the breeds, and prohibiting the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle.
sections.cm:
The State shall organise farming and animal husbandry on modern, scientific lines. The State shall preserve and improve breeds, and ban the slaughter of cows, calves and other milch and draught cattle.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
States defend their laws on cattle slaughter under Article 48, read with Article 48A.

In Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005) the Supreme Court upheld a total ban on cow slaughter, and overruled its own earlier position.

cl.name: State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat
cl.facts: Gujarat amended its law to impose a total ban on the slaughter of cows and their progeny of any age. Butchers challenged it as an unreasonable restriction on their trade under Article 19(1)(g).
cl.held: Upheld, overruling the earlier Mohd. Hanif Quareshi position that a total ban on bulls and bullocks past working age was unreasonable. The Court relied on Articles 48 and 48A and on Article 51A(g), and held the restriction reasonable in the public interest.
cl.why: The constitutional footing for the total cattle-slaughter bans now in force in several States, and a clear example of directive principles being used to justify a restriction on a fundamental right.

sections.t: Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life
sections.b:
The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011, s. 3 (w.e.f. 15-2-2012). 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, s. 3, for art. 45 3. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 10 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).]
sections.cm:
The State shall try to protect and improve the environment, and to safeguard the country's forests and wildlife.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 48A after the 1972 Stockholm Conference. The same amendment added Article 51A(g), the citizen's duty to protect the environment.

Courts read the two together into Article 21. In Subhash Kumar (1991) and the M.C. Mehta cases, the Court found an enforceable right to a clean environment. The polluter pays principle and the precautionary principle followed from the same reasoning.

sections.t: Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance
sections.b:
It shall be the obligation of the State to protect every monument or place or object of artistic or historic interest, 1[declared by or under law made by Parliament] to be of national importance, from spoliation, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal or export, as the case may be.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 27, for "declared by Parliament by law".]
sections.cm:
The State shall protect monuments, places and objects of artistic or historic interest that are declared to be of national importance.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 puts Article 49 into effect.

sections.t: Separation of judiciary from executive
sections.b: The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
sections.cm:
The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Before independence, a District Magistrate was both an administrator and a criminal judge. The officer who ordered an arrest could also try the case.

The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ended the overlap. Judicial magistrates under the High Court now try cases. Executive magistrates under the State government handle administration.

sections.t: Promotion of international peace and security
sections.b: The State shall endeavour to— (a) promote international peace and security; (b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations; (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another; and (d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
sections.cm:
The State shall promote international peace and security, and keep just and honourable relations between nations. The State shall also foster respect for international law and treaties, and encourage settling international disputes by arbitration.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A treaty India signs does not become Indian law by itself. Parliament must pass a law under Article 253 to give it effect.

But where Indian law is silent, courts use Article 51 to read international conventions in. In Vishaka (1997) the Court drew on the convention against discrimination towards women to lay down rules on sexual harassment at work.

sections.t: Fundamental duties
sections.b:
It shall be the duty of every citizen of India— (a) to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; (b) to cherish and follow the noble ideals which inspired our national struggle for freedom; (c) to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (d) to defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so; (e) to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; (f) to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture; (g) to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures; (h) to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; (i) to safeguard public property and to abjure violence; (j) to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement; ] 2[(k) who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 11 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). 2. Ins. by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, s. 4 (w.e.f. 1-4-2010).]
sections.cm:
Article 51A lists eleven duties of every citizen.

Respect the Constitution, the flag and the anthem. Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle. Uphold sovereignty and integrity. Defend the country. Promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to women. Value the composite culture. Protect the environment. Develop a scientific temper. Safeguard public property and abjure violence. Strive towards excellence. Provide education to your child between six and fourteen.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
No court can enforce a fundamental duty against a citizen. There is no writ and no general penalty.

But the duties are not decorative. Courts use them to interpret other provisions, and a duty can help show that a restriction under Article 19 is reasonable. Parliament has also made laws on several of them, such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.

cl.name: AIIMS Students' Union v. AIIMS
cl.facts: Institutional reservation in postgraduate medical admissions at AIIMS was challenged.
cl.held: Fundamental duties, though not enforceable by a writ, are as important as fundamental rights. Article 51A(j) — the duty to strive towards excellence — was read alongside the merit requirement, and the institutional preference was struck down as excessive.
cl.why: The clearest judicial statement that Article 51A is a legitimate interpretive tool rather than decoration.

sections.t: The President of India
sections.b: There shall be a President of India
sections.cm:
There shall be a President of India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 52 creates an elected head of state. A monarch inherits the office, but a President is chosen. So India is a republic, and since 1950 it has not been a dominion under the British Crown.

The President is the head of state, not the head of the government. The President represents the country, while the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers run the government.

sections.t: Executive power of the Union
sections.b: (1) The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution. (2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union shall be vested in the President and the exercise thereof shall be regulated by law. (3) Nothing in this article shall— (a) be deemed to transfer to the President any functions conferred by any existing law on the Government of any State or other authority; or (b) prevent Parliament from conferring by law functions on authorities other than the President.
sections.cm:
The executive power of the Union is vested in the President. The President uses it directly or through officers below the President. The President is also the supreme commander of the defence forces.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
"Vested in the President" is a formality. Read with Article 74, the power belongs to the President in name and to the Council of Ministers in substance.

Supreme command of the forces is likewise exercised as the law regulates it.

sections.t: Election of President
sections.b: The President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of— (a) the elected members of both Houses of Parliament; and (b) the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States. 1[Explanation.—In this article and in article 55, “State” includes the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union territory of *Puducherry.]
sections.cm:
The President is elected by an electoral college. The college has the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies, including those of Delhi and Puducherry.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Only elected members vote. Nominated members do not, and members of the Legislative Councils never do.

The votes also carry different values. Each State's weight follows its population, and the total value of all MLA votes equals the total value of all MP votes. So an MLA from Uttar Pradesh carries more weight than an MLA from Sikkim.

sections.t: Manner of election of President
sections.b:
(1) As far as practicable, there shall be uniformity in the scale of representation of the different States at the election of the President. (2) For the purpose of securing such uniformity among the States inter se as well as parity between the States as a whole and the Union, the number of votes which each elected member of Parliament and of the Legislative Assembly of each State is entitled to cast at such election shall be determined in the following manner:— (a) every elected member of the Legislative Assembly of a State shall have as many votes as there are multiples of one thousand in the quotient obtained by dividing the population of the State by the total number of the elected members of the Assembly; * Now Puducherry vide the Pondicherry (Alteration of Name) Act, 2006 (44 of 2006), s. 3 (b) if, after taking the said multiples of one thousand, the remainder is not less than five hundred, then the vote of each member referred to in sub-clause (a) shall be further increased by one; (c) each elected member of either House of Parliament shall have such number of votes as may be obtained by dividing the total number of votes assigned to the members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States under sub-clauses (a) and (b) by the total number of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament, fractions exceeding one-half being counted as one and other fractions being disregarded. (3) The election of the President shall be held in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and the voting at such election shall be by secret ballot. 1[Explanation.—In this article, the expression “population” means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published: Provided that the reference in this Explanation to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published shall, until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2[2026] have been published, be construed as a reference to the 1971 census.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Seventieth Amendment) Act, 1992, s. 2 (w.e.f. 1-6-1995).]
sections.cm:
The President's election must be as uniform as possible between the States, and balanced between the Union and the States.

Each MLA's vote is weighted by the State's population. Each MP's vote is weighted so that all MPs together equal all MLAs together. Voting is by the single transferable vote, in a secret ballot.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
"Population" here still means the 1971 census. The 42nd Amendment froze the figures, and the 84th extended the freeze until the first census after 2026.

So the value of a vote does not follow today's population at all.

sections.t: Term of office of President
sections.b:
(1) The President shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office: Provided that— (a) the President may, by writing under his hand addressed to the Vice-President, resign his office; (b) the President may, for violation of the Constitution, be removed from office by impeachment in the manner provided in article 61; (c) the President shall, notwithstanding the expiration of his term, continue to hold office until his successor enters upon his office. (2) Any resignation addressed to the Vice-President under clause (a) of the proviso to clause (1) shall forthwith be communicated by him to the Speaker of the House of the People. Explanation

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 12, for the 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001, s. 2, for "2000"]
sections.cm:
The President holds office for five years. The President may resign by writing to the Vice-President, and may be removed by impeachment under Article 61. The President stays in office until a successor takes over.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The last rule means the office is never vacant at the end of a term, whatever happens to the election timetable.

sections.t: Eligibility for re-election
sections.b: A person who holds, or who has held, office as President shall, subject to the other provisions of this Constitution, be eligible for re-election to that office.
sections.cm:
A person who has been President may stand for election again.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
There is no limit on the number of terms. Rajendra Prasad is the only President to have served two full terms.

sections.t: Qualifications for election as President
sections.b: (1) No person shall be eligible for election as President unless he— (a) is a citizen of India, (b) has completed the age of thirty-five years, and (c) is qualified for election as a member of the House of the People. (2) A person shall not be eligible for election as President if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State or under any local or other authority subject to the control of any of the said Governments. Explanation.—For the purposes of this article, a person shall not be deemed to hold any office of profit by reason only that he is the President or Vice-President of the Union or the Governor 1*** of any State or is a Minister either for the Union or for any State.
sections.cm:
A candidate for President must be a citizen of India, at least thirty-five years old, and qualified for election to the Lok Sabha. The candidate must hold no office of profit under the Union, a State or a local authority.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The President, the Vice-President, a Governor and a minister are expressly treated as not holding an office of profit. Without the exception, a sitting Vice-President could not stand.

sections.t: Conditions of President's office
sections.b: (1) The President shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State, and if a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State be elected President, he shall be deemed to have vacated his seat in that House on the date on which he enters upon his office as President. (2) The President shall not hold any other office of profit. (3) The President shall be entitled without payment of rent to the use of his official residences and shall be also entitled to such emoluments, allowances and privileges as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such emoluments, allowances and privileges as are specified in the Second Schedule. (4) The emoluments and allowances of the President shall not be diminished during his term of office.
sections.cm:
The President cannot be a member of either House of Parliament or of a State legislature. If a sitting member is elected President, the seat falls vacant.

The President gets a rent-free official residence and the pay set out in the Second Schedule, which cannot be cut during the term.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The bar on cutting the President's pay is a small but real guarantee of independence. No government can use the President's salary as a lever.

sections.t: Oath or affirmation by the President
sections.b:
Every President and every person acting as President or discharging the functions of the President shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe in the presence of the Chief Justice of India or, in his absence, the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court available, an oath or affirmation in the following form, that is to say— Amendment) "I, A.B., do swear in the name of God that I will faithfully execute the office solemnly affirm of President (or discharge the functions of the President) of India and will to the best of my ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law and that I will devote myself to the service and well-being of the people of India.".

[Editorial Notes: 1. The words "or Rajpramukh or Uparajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh]
sections.cm:
The President takes the oath before the Chief Justice of India. The President swears to carry out the office faithfully, to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and to serve the people of India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The promise to "preserve, protect and defend the Constitution" is what gives meaning to "violation of the Constitution", the only ground for impeachment under Article 61.

sections.t: Procedure for impeachment of the President
sections.b: (1) When a President is to be impeached for violation of the Constitution, the charge shall be preferred by either House of Parliament. (2) No such charge shall be preferred unless— (a) the proposal to prefer such charge is contained in a resolution which has been moved after at least fourteen days' notice in writing signed by not less than one-fourth of the total number of members of the House has been given of their intention to move the resolution, and (b) such resolution has been passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House. (3) When a charge has been so preferred by either House of Parliament, the other House shall investigate the charge or cause the charge to be investigated and the President shall have the right to appear and to be represented at such investigation. (4) If as a result of the investigation a resolution is passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of the House by which the charge was investigated or caused to be investigated, declaring that the charge preferred against the President has been sustained, such resolution shall have the effect of removing the President from his office as from the date on which the resolution is so passed.
sections.cm:
Impeachment has two stages.

First, either House brings a charge that the President has violated the Constitution. The charge needs fourteen days' written notice signed by a quarter of the House's members. The House must pass it by two-thirds of its total membership.

Then the other House investigates the charge. The President is removed if that House also upholds it by two-thirds of its total membership.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The only ground is "violation of the Constitution", and the Constitution never defines it. Misconduct, incompetence or illness alone is not enough. No President of India has ever faced the process.

The bodies that elect and remove the President also differ. Nominated members of Parliament cannot vote to elect a President, but they can vote to remove one. State Assemblies elect the President, but have no part in removal.

sections.t: Time of holding election to fill vacancy in the office of President and the term of office of person elected to fill casual vacancy
sections.b: (1) An election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the term of office of President shall be completed before the expiration of the term. (2) An election to fill a vacancy in the office of President occurring by reason of his death, resignation or removal, or otherwise shall be held as soon as possible after, and in no case later than six months from, the date of occurrence of the vacancy; and the person elected to fill the vacancy shall, subject to the provisions of article 56, be entitled to hold office for the full term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office.
sections.cm:
The election for a new President must be completed before the outgoing President's term ends. A vacancy caused by death, resignation or removal must be filled within six months.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A President elected to fill such a vacancy gets a full five-year term, not the rest of the predecessor's term.

sections.t: The Vice-President of India
sections.b: There shall be a Vice-President of India
sections.cm:
There shall be a Vice-President of India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The office has almost no function of its own. Chairing the Rajya Sabha under Article 64 and acting as President under Article 65 are both borrowed roles.

So the Vice-President's real influence depends on how the Rajya Sabha is run.

sections.t: The Vice-President to be ex officio Chairman of the Council of States
sections.b: The Vice-President shall be ex officio Chairman of the Council of the States and shall not hold any other office of profit: Provided that during any period when the Vice-President acts as President or discharges the functions of the President under article 65, he shall not perform the duties of the office of Chairman of the Council of States and shall not be entitled to any salary or allowance payable to the Chairman of the Council of States under article 97.
sections.cm:
The Vice-President is, by virtue of the office, Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. While acting as President, the Vice-President does not chair the House and draws no Chairman's salary.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Chairman is not a member of the House. So the Chairman has no ordinary vote, only a casting vote to break a tie.

sections.t: The Vice-President to act as President or to discharge his functions during casual vacancies in the office, or during the absence, of President
sections.b: (1) In the event of the occurrence of any vacancy in the office of the President by reason of his death, resignation or removal, or otherwise, the Vice-President shall act as President until the date on which a new President elected in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter to fill such vacancy enters upon his office. (2) When the President is unable to discharge his functions owing to absence, illness or any other cause, the Vice-President shall discharge his functions until the date on which the President resumes his duties. (3) The Vice-President shall, during, and in respect of, the period while he is so acting as, or discharging the functions of, President, have all the powers and immunities of the President and be entitled to such emoluments, allowances and privileges as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such emoluments, allowances and privileges as are specified in the Second Schedule.
sections.cm:
When the President's office is vacant, or the President cannot act, the Vice-President acts as President, with all the President's powers and immunities.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Constitution says nothing about what happens if both offices are vacant at once.

The President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 fills the gap. Under it the Chief Justice of India acts as President. But the rule comes from a statute, not from the Constitution.

sections.t: Election of Vice-President
sections.b:
(1) The Vice-President shall be elected by the 1[members of an electoral college consisting of the members of both Houses of Parliament] in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and the voting at such election shall be by secret ballot. (2) The Vice-President shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State, and if a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State be elected Vice-President, he shall be deemed to have vacated his seat in that House on the date on which he enters upon his office as Vice-President. (3) No person shall be eligible for election as Vice-President unless he— (a) is a citizen of India; (b) has completed the age of thirty-five years; and Houses of Parliament assembled at a joint meeting" (c) is qualified for election as a member of the Council of States. (4) A person shall not be eligible for election as Vice-President if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State or under any local or other authority subject to the control of any of the said Governments. Explanation.—For the purposes of this article, a person shall not be deemed to hold any office of profit by reason only that he is the President or Vice-President of the Union or the Governor 1*** of any State or is a Minister either for the Union or for any State.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Eleventh Amendment) Act, 1961, s. 2, for "members of both]
sections.cm:
The Vice-President is elected by the members of both Houses of Parliament. They vote by proportional representation through the single transferable vote, in a secret ballot.

A candidate must be a citizen, at least 35 years old, and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The election differs from the President's in two ways. Nominated members of Parliament vote, and the State Assemblies play no part at all.

So the Vice-President is chosen by Parliament alone.

sections.t: Term of office of Vice-President
sections.b: The Vice-President shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office: Provided that— (a) a Vice-President may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office; (b) a Vice-President may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council of States passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council and agreed to by the House of the People; but no resolution for the purpose of this clause shall be moved unless at least fourteen days' notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution; (c) a Vice-President shall, notwithstanding the expiration of his term, continue to hold office until his successor enters upon his office.
sections.cm:
The Vice-President holds office for five years, and may resign by writing to the President. The Vice-President may be removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution, passed by a majority of all its then members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Only fourteen days' notice is needed, and no ground has to be stated.

So removing a Vice-President is far easier than impeaching a President, which needs two-thirds of the total membership of each House.

sections.t: Time of holding election to fill vacancy in the office of Vice-President and the term of office of person elected to fill casual vacancy
sections.b: (1) An election to fill a vacancy caused by the expiration of the term of office of Vice-President shall be completed before the expiration of the term. (2) An election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President occurring by reason of his death, resignation or removal, or otherwise shall be held as soon as possible after the occurrence of the vacancy, and the person elected to fill the vacancy shall, subject to the provisions of article 67, be entitled to hold office for the full term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office.
sections.cm:
An election to fill the Vice-President's office must be completed before the outgoing Vice-President's term ends. A vacancy for any other reason must be filled as soon as possible.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Nobody acts as Vice-President during a vacancy. The presidency, by contrast, is always filled under Article 65. In the meantime the Rajya Sabha's Deputy Chairman simply presides.

sections.t: Oath or affirmation by the Vice-President
sections.b:
Every Vice-President shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe before the Amendment) President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation in the following form, that is to say— "I, A.B., do swear in the name of God that I will bear true faith and solemnly affirm allegiance to as by law established and that I will faithfully discharge the duty upon which I am about to enter.".

[Editorial Notes: 1. The words "or Rajpramukh or Uparajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh]
sections.cm:
The Vice-President takes the oath before the President. The Vice-President swears true faith and allegiance to the Constitution, and to carry out the duties of the office faithfully.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Compare Article 60. The Vice-President makes no promise to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution, because the office carries no executive charge.

sections.t: Discharge of President's functions in other contingencies
sections.b: Parliament may make such provision as it thinks fit for the discharge of the functions of the President in any contingency not provided for in this Chapter.
sections.cm:
Parliament may provide for the President's functions to be carried out in any situation the Constitution does not cover.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 was made under Article 70.

sections.t: Matters relating to, or connected with, the election of a President or Vice-President
sections.b: (1) All doubts and disputes arising out of or in connection with the election of a President or Vice-President shall be inquired into and decided by the Supreme Court whose decision shall be final. (2) If the election of a person as President or Vice-President is declared void by the Supreme Court, acts done by him in the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office of President or Vice-President, as the case may be, on or before the date of the decision of the Supreme Court shall not be invalidated by reason of that declaration. (3) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may by law regulate any matter relating to or connected with the election of a President or Vice-President. (4) The election of a person as President or Vice-President shall not be called in question on the ground of the existence of any vacancy for whatever reason among the members of the electoral college electing him.]
sections.cm:
All doubts and disputes about the election of a President or Vice-President go to the Supreme Court, whose decision is final.

An election cannot be set aside only because the electoral college had vacancies. And acts done before an election is set aside remain valid.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 39th Amendment (1975) tried to take these disputes away from the courts. The 44th Amendment (1978) gave them back to the Supreme Court.

sections.t: Power of President to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases
sections.b:
(1) The President shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence— (a) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is by a Court Martial; further (2) Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the power conferred by law on any officer of the Armed Forces of the Union to suspend, remit or commute a sentence passed by a Court Martial. (3) Nothing in sub-clause (c) of clause (1) shall affect the power to suspend, remit or commute a sentence of death exercisable by the Governor 1*** of a State under any law for the time being in force.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 2 (w.e.f 10-8-1975) and subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 10. (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). (b) in all cases where the punishment or sentence is for an offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends; (c) in all cases where the sentence is a sentence of death.]
sections.cm:
The President may pardon a convict, or suspend, remit or commute a sentence.

The power covers sentences by a court martial, offences against Union laws, and every death sentence.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The President acts on the government's advice. So a mercy decision is really the government's decision.

Courts will not weigh the merits again. But Epuru Sudhakar (2006) held that a decision can be struck down if it is arbitrary, made in bad faith, or based on irrelevant grounds. And Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) held that a long, unexplained delay in deciding a mercy petition is itself a ground to commute a death sentence.

cl.name: Kehar Singh v. Union of India
cl.facts: A convict sentenced to death for the assassination of Indira Gandhi filed a mercy petition, asking the President to reconsider the evidence.
cl.held: The President may examine the evidence afresh and take a different view from the court, because the pardon power is an executive act of grace and not a judicial appeal. He is not obliged to give a hearing or reasons, and the order need not be a speaking one.
cl.why: It defined the pardon power as independent of the judicial record — while confirming it is exercised on the government's advice, not personally.

cl.name: Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh
cl.facts: The Governor remitted the sentence of a Congress worker convicted of murder, on grounds the petitioner said were false and politically motivated.
cl.held: The pardon power is subject to judicial review — not on the merits, but where the order is passed without applying mind, on wholly irrelevant grounds, in bad faith, or by suppressing material facts. The remission was set aside.
cl.why: It ended the idea that clemency is wholly beyond the courts, while keeping the Court out of second-guessing the decision itself.

cl.name: Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India
cl.facts: Death-row convicts whose mercy petitions had lain undecided for years — in one case over eleven — sought commutation on grounds of delay and mental illness.
cl.held: Inordinate and unexplained delay in deciding a mercy petition is itself a ground to commute a death sentence to life imprisonment, because the agony of waiting violates Article 21. Insanity and solitary confinement are further grounds.
cl.why: Fifteen death sentences were commuted, and the Court laid down execution guidelines — a 14-day gap after rejection, legal aid, a final family meeting.

sections.t: Extent of executive power of the Union
sections.b:
(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the executive power of the Union shall extend— (a) to the matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws; and (b) to the exercise of such rights, authority and jurisdiction as are exercisable by the Government of India by virtue of any treaty or agreement: Provided that the executive power referred to in sub-clause (a) shall not, save as expressly provided in this Constitution or in any law made by Parliament, extend in any State 2*** to matters with respect to which the Legislature of the State has also power to make laws. (2) Until otherwise provided by Parliament, a State and any officer or authority of a State may, notwithstanding anything in this article, continue to exercise in matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws for that State such executive power or functions as the State or officer or authority thereof could exercise immediately before the commencement of this Constitution.

[Editorial Notes: 1. The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. 2. The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch.]
sections.cm:
The executive power of the Union covers every matter on which Parliament can make laws, and the rights and powers India holds under a treaty.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
But the Union's executive power does not reach matters where a State has executive power, unless the Constitution or a law of Parliament says so. Article 162 sets the same rule from the State's side.

sections.t: Council of Ministers to aid and advise President
sections.b: 1[(1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice:] 2[Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.] (2) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the President shall not be inquired into in any court.
sections.cm:
A Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister, aids and advises the President. The President must act on that advice.
