The President may send the advice back once for reconsideration. But the President must then accept whatever advice comes back.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The binding words came later. Until 1976 the text said only that the Council would "aid and advise", and some argued that the President could refuse. The 42nd Amendment (1976) settled the question by adding "shall act in accordance with such advice". The 44th Amendment (1978) then let the President return the advice once.

Clause (2) shields the advice itself. No court may ask what the ministers told the President. But S.R. Bommai (1994) held that the material behind a decision can still be examined.

Practitioner Note:
The President's main remaining discretion is the pocket veto. Article 111 sets no time limit for assent. In 1986 President Zail Singh used the gap to hold back the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.

cl.name: Samsher Singh v. State of Punjab
cl.facts: A probationary judicial officer's services were terminated by an order issued in the Governor's name but decided by the government. He argued the Governor had to decide personally.
cl.held: The President and the Governor are constitutional heads who act only on the aid and advice of their Council of Ministers, except in the few areas where the Constitution expressly requires personal discretion. India follows the Westminster convention.
cl.why: The definitive statement that executive power in India is exercised by the Cabinet, decided two years before the 42nd Amendment made the same point in the text of Article 74.

sections.t: Other provisions as to Ministers
sections.b:
(1) The Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. 3[(1A) The total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed fifteen per cent. of the total number of members of the House of the People. (1B) A member of either House of Parliament belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of that House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified to be appointed as a Minister under clause (1) for duration of the period commencing from the date of his disqualification till the date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or where he contests any election to either House of Parliament before the expiry of such period, till the date on which he is declared elected, whichever is earlier.] (2) The Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. (3) The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People. (4) Before a Minister enters upon his office, the President shall administer to him the oaths of office and of secrecy according to the forms set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule. (5) A Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of either House of Parliament shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister. (6) The salaries and allowances of Ministers shall be such as Parliament may from time to time by law determine and, until Parliament so determines, shall be as specified in the Second Schedule.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s.13, for cl. (1) 2. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 11 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). 3. Ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 2 (w.e.f. 1-1-2004).]
sections.cm:
The President appoints the Prime Minister, and appoints the other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice.

The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure. A minister who is not a member of either House must become one within six months.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Ministers hold office "during the pleasure of the President". But the President cannot dismiss a minister who keeps the Prime Minister's confidence. So in practice the Prime Minister decides who stays.

The 91st Amendment (2003) added two limits. Clause (1A) caps the Council at 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha's strength, to stop large ministries being used to buy loyalty. Clause (1B) bars a member disqualified for defection from becoming a minister until re-elected.

cl.name: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
cl.facts: Karnataka's Chief Minister was dismissed after the Governor reported he had lost his majority, relying on letters of withdrawal — without a floor test. Several other dismissals were challenged with it.
cl.held: The only constitutionally valid test of a government's majority is a vote on the floor of the House, not the Governor's assessment in Raj Bhavan.
cl.why: The floor test is now the automatic judicial answer whenever a State government's majority is disputed, from Uttarakhand in 2016 to Maharashtra in 2022.

cl.name: Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker, Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly
cl.facts: Twenty-two Congress MLAs resigned in Madhya Pradesh. The Governor directed a floor test; the Speaker adjourned the House citing the pandemic; the opposition asked the Court to order an immediate test.
cl.held: The Governor may call for a floor test where there is objective material suggesting the government has lost confidence, but he cannot use the power to dislodge a government on his own assessment. The Court ordered the test to be held the next day.
cl.why: It tightened Bommai into a workable rule about when a Governor may act and how fast a disputed majority must be tested.

sections.t: Attorney-General for India
sections.b: (1) The President shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of the Supreme Court to be Attorney-General for India. (2) It shall be the duty of the Attorney-General to give advice to the Government of India upon such legal matters, and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the President, and to discharge the functions conferred on him by or under this Constitution or any other law for the time being in force. (3) In the performance of his duties the Attorney-General shall have right of audience in all courts in the territory of India. (4) The Attorney-General shall hold office during the pleasure of the President, and shall receive such remuneration as the President may determine.
sections.cm:
The President appoints the Attorney-General for India. The person must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge.

The Attorney-General advises the Government of India on legal matters and may appear in any court in India. The Attorney-General may also speak in either House of Parliament, but cannot vote.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The office has no fixed term and no removal procedure. The Attorney-General holds office during the President's pleasure, and by convention resigns when the government changes.

The Attorney-General is also not a full-time government lawyer, and is not a minister. Private practice is allowed, though not against the Government of India.

sections.t: Conduct of business of the Government of India
sections.b:
(1) All executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President. (2) Orders and other instruments made and executed in the name of the President shall be authenticated in such manner as may be specified in rules1 to be made by the President, and the validity of an order or instrument which is so authenticated shall not be called in question on the ground that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the President. (3) The President shall make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of India, and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business. 2(4) * * * * Extraordinary, Pt. II, Sec. 3 (ii), p. 1315, as amended from time to time.

[Editorial Notes: 1. See notifin No. S.O. 2297, dated the 3rd November, 1958, Gazette of India, 2. Cl. (4) was ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s.14 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977) and omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 12 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).]
sections.cm:
All executive action of the Union is taken in the President's name. An order signed in the prescribed way cannot be challenged on the ground that the President did not make it.

The President makes rules dividing the government's business among the ministers.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 77 is the legal machinery of Cabinet government. The Allocation of Business Rules and the Transaction of Business Rules both come from clause (3).

sections.t: Duties of Prime Minister as respects the furnishing of information to the President, etc
sections.b: It shall be the duty of the Prime Minister— (a) to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation; (b) to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the Union and proposals for legislation as the President may call for; and (c) if the President so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.
sections.cm:
The Prime Minister has three duties towards the President.

The Prime Minister must report all decisions of the Council of Ministers on administration and legislation. The Prime Minister must give any information on those matters that the President asks for. And if the President asks, the Prime Minister must put a decision taken by one minister alone before the whole Council.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The President has no machinery of government of their own. So Article 78 is the main way the President learns what the government is doing.

But the right is to know, not to decide. The President can make the whole Council look at a minister's decision again, but cannot make it change the decision.

sections.t: Constitution of Parliament
sections.b: There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.
sections.cm:
Parliament consists of the President and two Houses. The Houses are the Council of States, or Rajya Sabha, and the House of the People, or Lok Sabha.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The President is part of Parliament, though the President sits in neither House. The American President, by contrast, stands wholly outside Congress.

So a Bill becomes law only when the President assents. The President also summons and prorogues the Houses, and dissolves the Lok Sabha.

sections.t: Composition of the Council of States
sections.b:
(1) 1[2*** The Council of States] shall consist of— (a) twelve members to be nominated by the President in accordance with the provisions of clause (3); and (b) not more than two hundred and thirty-eight representatives of the States 3[and of the Union territories]. (2) The allocation of seats in the Council of States to be filled by representatives of the States 3[and of the Union territories] shall be in accordance with the provisions in that behalf contained in the Fourth Schedule. (3) The members to be nominated by the President under sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall consist of persons having special knowledge or practical experience in respect of such matters as the following, namely:— Literature, science, art and social service. of States" Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 5 (4) The representatives of each State 1*** in the Council of States shall be elected by the elected members of the Legislative Assembly of the State in accordance with the system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote. (5) The representatives of the 2[Union territories] in the Council of States shall be chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law prescribe.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1974, s. 3, for "The Council 2. The words "Subject to the provisions of para. 4 of the Tenth Schedule," omitted by the 3. Added by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 3 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).]
sections.cm:
The Rajya Sabha has up to 238 members representing the States and Union territories, and twelve members nominated by the President.

The elected members of each State Assembly choose that State's members, by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. The President nominates people with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Seats are allotted in the Fourth Schedule, roughly by population. Uttar Pradesh has 31 seats and Sikkim has one. So, unlike the American Senate, the House of the States does not treat the States equally.

Until 2003 a candidate had to live in the State they sought to represent. An amendment to the Representation of the People Act dropped the rule, and the Court upheld the change in Kuldip Nayar (2006).

sections.t: Composition of the House of the People
sections.b:
(1) 4[Subject to the provisions of article 331 5***], the House of the People shall consist of— (a) not more than 6[five hundred and thirty members] chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States; and (b) not more than 7[twenty members] to represent the Union territories, chosen in such manner as Parliament may by law provide. (2) For the purposes of sub-clause (a) of clause (1),— (a) there shall be allotted to each State a number of seats in the House of the People in such manner that the ratio between that number and the population of the State is, so far as practicable, the same for all States; and (b) each State shall be divided into territorial constituencies in such manner that the ratio between the population of each constituency and the number of seats allotted to it is, so far as practicable, the same throughout the State: 8[Provided that the provisions of sub-clause (a) of this clause shall not be applicable for the purpose of allotment of seats in the House of the People to any State so long as the population of that State does not exceed six millions.] the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 3 provisions of art. 331" (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 5 "five hundred and twenty-five members" members" (3) In this article, the expression “population” means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published: 1[Provided that the reference in this clause to the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published shall, until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2[2026] have been published, 3[be construed,— (i) for the purposes of sub-clause (a) of clause (2) and the proviso to that clause, as a reference to the 1971 census; and (ii) for the purposes of sub-clause (b) of clause (2) as a reference to the 4[2001] census.]]

[Editorial Notes: 1. The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by 2. Subs. by s. 3, ibid, for "States specified in Part C of First Schedule" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956). 3. Subs. by s. 4, ibid. for arts. 81 and 82 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956). 4. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1974, s. 4, for "subject to the 5. The words and figure "and para. 4 of the Tenth Schedule" omitted by the Constitution 6. Subs. by the Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987 (18 of 1987), s. 63, for 7. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirty-first Amendment) Act, 1973, s. 2, for "twenty-five 8. Ins. by s. 2, ibid. (w.e.f. 17-10-1973).]
sections.cm:
The Lok Sabha has up to 530 members from the States and up to 20 from the Union territories. All are directly elected from territorial constituencies.

Seats are shared so that each State's ratio of seats to population is, as far as practicable, the same.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
"Population" here still means the 1971 census. Without a freeze, States that had slowed their population growth would have lost seats to States that had not.

So the 42nd Amendment froze the State-wise totals on 1971 figures. The 84th Amendment extended the freeze until the first census after 2026. The 87th let boundaries inside each State be redrawn on 2001 figures, and the new boundaries took effect in 2008.

sections.t: Readjustment after each census
sections.b:
Upon the completion of each census, the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States and the division of each State into territorial constituencies shall be readjusted by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law determine: Provided that such readjustment shall not affect representation in the House of the People until the dissolution of the then existing House: 5[Provided further that such readjustment shall take effect from such date as the President may, by order, specify and until such readjustment takes effect, any election to the House may be held on the basis of the territorial constituencies existing before such readjustment: Provided also that until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 6[2026] have been published, it shall not be necessary to 7[readjust,— (i) the allocation of seats in the House of the People to the States as readjusted on the basis of the 1971 census; and (ii) the division of each State into territorial constituencies as may be readjusted on the basis of the 1[2001] census, under this article.]]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Added by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 15 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001, s. 3, for "2000" 3. Subs. by s.3, ibid, for certain words (w.e.f. 21-2-2002). 4. Subs. by the Constitution (Eighty-seventh Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 2, for "1991" 5. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 16 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). 6. Subs. by the Constitution (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001, s. 4, for "2000" 7. Subs. by s.4, ibid., for certain words (w.e.f. 21-2-2002).]
sections.cm:
After every census, Parliament shall by law readjust how Lok Sabha seats are shared among the States, and how each State is divided into constituencies.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The provisos put off any change in the sharing of seats until after the first census taken after 2026.

So delimitation will be one of the sharpest questions between the Union and the States in the coming decade.

sections.t: Duration of Houses of Parliament
sections.b: (1) The Council of States shall not be subject to dissolution, but as nearly as possible one-third of the members thereof shall retire as soon as may be on the expiration of every second year in accordance with the provisions made in that behalf by Parliament by law. (2) The House of the People, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for 2[five years] from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of 2[five years] shall operate as a dissolution of the House: Provided that the said period may, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, be extended by Parliament by law for a period not exceeding one year at a time and not extending in any case beyond a period of six months after the Proclamation has ceased to operate.
sections.cm:
The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved. One-third of its members retire every second year.

The Lok Sabha lasts five years from its first sitting, unless dissolved sooner. During an emergency, Parliament may extend its life by a year at a time. But any extension ends six months after the emergency ends.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) stretched the Lok Sabha's term to six years. The 44th Amendment (1978) brought it back to five.

The emergency extension has been used once. The Lok Sabha elected in 1971 was extended twice during the 1975 Emergency, and ran on into 1977.

sections.t: Qualification for membership of Parliament
sections.b:
A person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in Parliament unless he— 3[(a) is a citizen of India, and makes and subscribes before some person authorised in that behalf by the Election Commission an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule;] (b) is, in the case of a seat in the Council of States, not less than thirty years of age and, in the case of a seat in the House of the People, not less than twenty-five years of age; and (c) possesses such other qualifications as may be prescribed in that behalf by or under any law made by Parliament.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Eighty-seventh Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 3, for "1991" 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 17, for "five years" 3. Subs. by the Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, s. 3, for cl.(a)]
sections.cm:
A member of Parliament must be a citizen and take the prescribed oath. A member must be at least thirty for the Rajya Sabha, or twenty-five for the Lok Sabha. Parliament may add further qualifications.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Constitution sets only a floor. The disqualifications that decide most real cases come from statute, mainly section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

In Lily Thomas (2013) the Court held that disqualification on conviction takes effect at once. A pending appeal gives no protection.

sections.t: Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution
sections.b: (1) The President shall from time to time summon each House of Parliament to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit, but six months shall not intervene between its last sitting in one session and the date appointed for its first sitting in the next session. (2) The President may from time to time— (a) prorogue the Houses or either House; (b) dissolve the House of the People.]
sections.cm:
The President summons each House from time to time. No more than six months may pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next.

The President may also prorogue the Houses, and dissolve the Lok Sabha.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The rule fixes only a maximum gap between sessions. The rule does not require three sessions a year, or any minimum number of sitting days. The three sessions are a convention.

So nothing in Article 85 stops sitting days from falling, and they have fallen steadily over the decades.

sections.t: Right of President to address and send messages to Houses
sections.b: (1) The President may address either House of Parliament or both Houses assembled together, and for that purpose require the attendance of members. (2) The President may send messages to either House of Parliament, whether with respect to a Bill then pending in Parliament or otherwise, and a House to which any message is so sent shall with all convenient despatch consider any matter required by the message to be taken into consideration.
sections.cm:
The President may address either House, or both together. The President may also send a message to a House about a pending Bill or anything else, and the House must consider it promptly.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The power to send a message has never been used. The power to address is used on the government's advice, and the government writes the address.

sections.t: Special address by the President
sections.b: (1) At the commencement of 2[the first session after each general election to the House of the People and at the commencement of the first session of each year] the President shall address both Houses of Parliament assembled together and inform Parliament of the causes of its summons. (2) Provision shall be made by the rules regulating the procedure of either House for the allotment of time for discussion of the matters referred to in such address 3***.
sections.cm:
The President addresses both Houses together at the first session after each general election, and at the first session of each year. The address gives the reasons for summoning Parliament.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The government writes the address, and the President reads it. Parliament debates it through the Motion of Thanks.

The Motion works as a test of confidence. A government that lost the vote would be in serious trouble.

sections.t: Rights of Ministers and Attorney-General as respects Houses
sections.b:
Every Minister and the Attorney-General of India shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, either House, any joint sitting of the Houses, and any committee of Parliament of which he may be named a member, but shall not by virtue of this article be entitled to vote.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s. 6, for art. 85 2. Subs. by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s. 7, for "every session" 3. The words "and for the precedence of such discussion over other business of the House" (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). omitted by s. 7, ibid. (w.e.f. 18-6-1951).]
sections.cm:
Every minister and the Attorney-General may speak and take part in the proceedings of either House, and of any committee they are named to.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
So a minister who sits in the Rajya Sabha can steer a Bill through the Lok Sabha.

But a minister can never vote in a House they do not belong to, not even on their own Bill.

sections.t: The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States
sections.b: (1) The Vice-President of India shall be ex officio Chairman of the Council of States. (2) The Council of States shall, as soon as may be, choose a member of the Council to be Deputy Chairman thereof and, so often as the office of Deputy Chairman becomes vacant, the Council shall choose another member to be Deputy Chairman thereof.
sections.cm:
The Vice-President is, by virtue of the office, Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The House chooses a Deputy Chairman from among its own members.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Chairman is not a member of the House. The Chairman's whole authority over the Rajya Sabha comes from Article 89, and the Chairman votes only to break a tie.

sections.t: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the office of Deputy Chairman
sections.b: A member holding office as Deputy Chairman of the Council of States— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the Council; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the Council passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council: Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution.
sections.cm:
The Deputy Chairman leaves office on ceasing to be a member, or on resigning by writing to the Chairman. The House may also remove the Deputy Chairman, by a resolution passed by a majority of all its then members after fourteen days' notice.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A majority of all the then members is a higher bar than a majority of those present and voting.

sections.t: Power of the Deputy Chairman or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Chairman
sections.b: (1) While the office of Chairman is vacant, or during any period when the Vice-President is acting as, or discharging the functions of, President, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Chairman, or, if the office of Deputy Chairman is also vacant, by such member of the Council of States as the President may appoint for the purpose. (2) During the absence of the Chairman from any sitting of the Council of States the Deputy Chairman, or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the Council, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the Council, shall act as Chairman.
sections.cm:
The Deputy Chairman does the Chairman's work while the Chairman's office is vacant. If both are unavailable, a member appointed by the President does it.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
When the Vice-President is acting as President, the Deputy Chairman runs the Rajya Sabha. So the office matters more than its ceremonial description suggests.

sections.t: The Chairman or the Deputy Chairman not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
sections.b: (1) At any sitting of the Council of States, while any resolution for the removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration, the Chairman, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Chairman from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Chairman, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 91 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Chairman, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Chairman, is absent. (2) The Chairman shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take removal of the Vice-President from his office is under consideration in the Council, but, notwithstanding anything in article 100, shall not be entitled to vote at all on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings.
sections.cm:
While a resolution to remove the Chairman or the Deputy Chairman is being considered, that person cannot preside.

The Chairman may still speak and take part in the proceedings. But the Chairman may not vote at all while the resolution is being considered, on it or on anything else.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Lok Sabha Speaker is treated differently. Under Article 96 a Speaker facing removal may vote in the first instance, because the Speaker is a member of the House. The Chairman is not.

sections.t: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People
sections.b: The House of the People shall, as soon as may be, choose two members of the House to be respectively Speaker and Deputy Speaker thereof and, so often as the office of Speaker or Deputy Speaker becomes vacant, the House shall choose another member to be Speaker or Deputy Speaker, as the case may be.
sections.cm:
The Lok Sabha chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker, "as soon as may be". When either office falls vacant, the House chooses another member.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The words "as soon as may be" set no deadline. So the Deputy Speaker's post can stay empty for years, and it stayed empty through the whole of the seventeenth Lok Sabha.

The Deputy Speaker's post also falls vacant when the House is dissolved. But the Speaker stays in office until just before the new House first meets, so the chair is never empty.

sections.t: Vacation and resignation of, and removal from, the offices of Speaker and Deputy Speaker
sections.b: A member holding office as Speaker or Deputy Speaker of the House of the People— (a) shall vacate his office if he ceases to be a member of the House of the People; (b) may at any time, by writing under his hand addressed, if such member is the Speaker, to the Deputy Speaker, and if such member is the Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker, resign his office; and (c) may be removed from his office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then members of the House: Provided that no resolution for the purpose of clause (c) shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution: Provided further that, whenever the House of the People is dissolved, the Speaker shall not vacate his office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.
sections.cm:
The Speaker or Deputy Speaker leaves office on ceasing to be a member of the House, or on resigning. Either can also be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, after fourteen days' notice.

The Speaker does not leave office when the House is dissolved. The Speaker stays until just before the new House first meets.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
While a resolution to remove the Speaker is being considered, the Speaker cannot preside. But the Speaker may speak in the debate and vote in the first instance, though not cast a deciding vote.

The Speaker who stays on after dissolution is a deliberate design. So the House always has a presiding officer, even between two Lok Sabhas.

sections.t: Power of the Deputy Speaker or other person to perform the duties of the office of, or to act as, Speaker
sections.b: (1) While the office of Speaker is vacant, the duties of the office shall be performed by the Deputy Speaker or, if the office of Deputy Speaker is also vacant, by such member of the House of the People as the President may appoint for the purpose. (2) During the absence of the Speaker from any sitting of the House of the People the Deputy Speaker or, if he is also absent, such person as may be determined by the rules of procedure of the House, or, if no such person is present, such other person as may be determined by the House, shall act as Speaker.
sections.cm:
The Deputy Speaker does the Speaker's work while the Speaker's office is vacant. If both offices are vacant, a member appointed by the President does it.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
When the Speaker is only absent from a sitting, the Deputy Speaker presides. If the Deputy Speaker is absent too, a member from a panel that the Speaker names in advance takes the chair.

sections.t: The Speaker or the Deputy Speaker not to preside while a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration
sections.b: (1) At any sitting of the House of the People, while any resolution for the removal of the Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Speaker, or while any resolution for the removal of the Deputy Speaker from his office is under consideration, the Deputy Speaker, shall not, though he is present, preside, and the provisions of clause (2) of article 95 shall apply in relation to every such sitting as they apply in relation to a sitting from which the Speaker, or, as the case may be, the Deputy Speaker, is absent. (2) The Speaker shall have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, the House of the People while any resolution for his removal from office is under consideration in the House and shall, notwithstanding anything in article 100, be entitled to vote only in the first instance on such resolution or on any other matter during such proceedings but not in the case of an equality of votes.
sections.cm:
A Speaker or Deputy Speaker whose removal is being considered cannot preside over that sitting. The Speaker may still speak, and may vote in the first instance, though not cast a deciding vote.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Nabam Rebia (2016) added a further rule. A Speaker facing a notice for removal should not decide petitions to disqualify members for defection. In 2023 the Court sent that rule to a larger bench to reconsider.

sections.t: Salaries and allowances of the Chairman and Deputy Chairman and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker
sections.b: There shall be paid to the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, and to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, such salaries and allowances as may be respectively fixed by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries and allowances as are specified in the Second Schedule.
sections.cm:
The Chairman, Deputy Chairman, Speaker and Deputy Speaker receive the salaries and allowances Parliament fixes. The money is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Charged spending is not put to a vote in Parliament. So the presiding officers' pay is kept out of the yearly fight over the Budget.

sections.t: Secretariat of Parliament
sections.b: (1) Each House of Parliament shall have a separate secretarial staff: Provided that nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the creation of posts common to both Houses of Parliament. (2) Parliament may by law regulate the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of either House of Parliament. (3) Until provision is made by Parliament under clause (2), the President may, after consultation with the Speaker of the House of the People or the Chairman of the Council of States, as the case may be, make rules regulating the recruitment, and the conditions of service of persons appointed, to the secretarial staff of the House of the People or the Council of States, and any rules so made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any law made under the said clause.
sections.cm:
Each House has its own secretarial staff. Parliament may make laws on how the staff are recruited and on their conditions of service.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Separate staff is a small but real guarantee of independence. Each House recruits its own employees, so the executive does not control them.

sections.t: Oath or affirmation by members
sections.b: Every member of either House of Parliament shall, before taking his seat, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule.
sections.cm:
Every member must take an oath or affirmation before taking a seat. The oath is taken before the President, or a person the President appoints, in the form set out in the Third Schedule.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Until the oath is taken, a member cannot sit or vote, and Article 104 imposes a penalty on one who does. So a member-elect who delays the oath has no voice in the House at all.

sections.t: Voting in Houses, power of Houses to act notwithstanding vacancies and quorum
sections.b: (1) Save as otherwise provided in this Constitution, all questions at any sitting of either House or joint sitting of the Houses shall be determined by a majority of votes of the members present and voting, other than the Speaker or person acting as Chairman or Speaker. The Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, shall not vote in the first instance, but shall have and exercise a casting vote in the case of an equality of votes. (2) Either House of Parliament shall have power to act notwithstanding any vacancy in the membership thereof, and any proceedings in Parliament shall be valid notwithstanding that it is discovered subsequently that some person who was not entitled so to do sat or voted or otherwise took part in the proceedings. 1[(3) Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament shall be one-tenth of the total number of members of the House. (4) If at any time during a meeting of a House there is no quorum, it shall be the duty of the Chairman or Speaker, or person acting as such, either to adjourn the House or to suspend the meeting until there is a quorum.]
sections.cm:
Questions in a House are decided by a majority of the members present and voting. The presiding officer does not vote, except to break a tie.

A House can act even when it has vacancies. The quorum is one-tenth of the total membership.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
One-tenth is a very low quorum, about fifty-five members in the Lok Sabha.

The presiding officer need not count heads unless a member points out that the House lacks a quorum.

sections.t: Vacation of seats
sections.b:
(1) No person shall be a member of both Houses of Parliament and provision shall be made by Parliament by law for the vacation by a person who is chosen a member of both Houses of his seat in one House or the other. (2) No person shall be a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of a State 1***, and if a person is chosen a member both of Parliament and of a House of the Legislature of 2[a State], then, at the expiration of such period as may be specified in rules* made by the President, that person’s seat in Parliament shall become vacant, unless he has previously resigned his seat in the Legislature of the State. (3) If a member of either House of Parliament— (a) becomes subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in 3[clause (1) or clause (2) of article 102]; or 4[(b) resigns his seat by writing under his hand addressed to the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, and his resignation is accepted by the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be,] his seat shall thereupon become vacant: 5[Provided that in the case of any resignation referred to in sub-clause (b), if from information received or otherwise and after making such inquiry as he thinks fit, the Chairman or the Speaker, as the case may be, is satisfied that such resignation is not voluntary or genuine, he shall not accept such resignation.] (4) If for a period of sixty days a member of either House of Parliament is without permission of the House absent from all meetings thereof, the House may declare his seat vacant: Provided that in computing the said period of sixty days no account shall be taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days. the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) * See the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950, published with the Ministry of Law, notifn. No. F. 46/50-C, dated the 26th January, 1950, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, P. 678. 102"

[Editorial Notes: 1. The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by 2. Subs. by s. 29 and Sch., ibid., for "such a State" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956). 3. Subs. by the Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985, s. 2, for "cl. (1) of art. 4. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirty-third Amendment) Act, 1974, s. 2 (w.e.f. 19-5-1974). 5. Ins. by s.2, ibid. (w.e.f. 19-5-1974). 1. Cls. (3) and (4) omitted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 18 (date not notified). This amendment was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 45 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).]
sections.cm:
Nobody may be a member of both Houses, or of Parliament and a State legislature, at the same time.

A seat falls vacant on disqualification, on resignation, or when a member stays away from all meetings for sixty days without permission.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Speaker or Chairman may refuse a resignation that is not voluntary and genuine.

The 33rd Amendment (1974) added the safeguard, after members were pressed into resigning during the agitations of that year.

sections.t: Disqualifications for membership
sections.b: (1) A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament— 1[(a) if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State, other than an office declared by Parliament by law not to disqualify its holder;] (b) if he is of unsound mind and stands so declared by a competent court; (c) if he is an undischarged insolvent; (d) if he is not a citizen of India, or has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State, or is under any acknowledgment of allegiance or adherence to a foreign State; (e) if he is so disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament. 2[Explanation.—For the purposes of this clause] a person shall not be deemed to hold an office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State by reason only that he is a Minister either for the Union or for such State. 3[(2) A person shall be disqualified for being a member of either House of Parliament if he is so disqualified under the Tenth Schedule.]
sections.cm:
A person is disqualified from Parliament for holding an office of profit under the Union or a State, for unsound mind, or for being an undischarged insolvent. A person is also disqualified for not being a citizen, for taking foreign citizenship, or under any law of Parliament.

Clause (2) adds disqualification for defection under the Tenth Schedule.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Constitution never defines an "office of profit".

Parliament has often exempted offices with retrospective effect, as it did in 2006 after the Jaya Bachchan case. So the test has become a political tool as much as a legal one.

sections.t: Decision on questions as to disqualifications of members
sections.b:
(1) If any question arises as to whether a member of either House of Parliament has become subject to any of the disqualifications mentioned in clause (1) of article 102, the question shall be referred for the decision of the President and his decision shall be final. he holds any such office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State as is declared by Parliament by law to disqualify its holder" (date not notified). (2) Before giving any decision on any such question, the President shall obtain the opinion of the Election Commission and shall act according to such opinion.]

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 19 to read as "(a) if 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985, s. 3, for "(2) for the 3. Ins. by s. 3, ibid. (w.e.f. 1-3-1985). 4. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 20, for art. 103 This amendment was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 45 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). purposes of this art." (w.e.f. 1-3-1985). (w.e.f. 3-1-1977) and further subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 14, for art. 103 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).]
sections.cm:
If a question arises whether a member is disqualified under Article 102(1), the President decides it. The President must first get the Election Commission's opinion, and must act on it.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Commission's opinion binds the President. Article 103 is one of the few places where an outside body's advice binds the head of State.

Disqualification for defection, under clause (2), is decided by the Speaker or Chairman instead.

sections.t: Penalty for sitting and voting before making oath or affirmation under article 99 or when not qualified or when disqualified
sections.b: If a person sits or votes as a member of either House of Parliament before he has complied with the requirements of article 99, or when he knows that he is not qualified or that he is disqualified for membership thereof, or that he is prohibited from so doing by the provisions of any law made by Parliament, he shall be liable in respect of each day on which he so sits or votes to a penalty of five hundred rupees to be recovered as a debt due to the Union.
sections.cm:
A member who sits or votes before taking the oath, while disqualified, or in breach of Article 101, must pay ₹500 for each such day. The sum is recovered as a debt owed to the Union.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The figure has not changed since 1950. The real deterrent is not the money but the disqualification that usually comes with it.

sections.t: Powers, privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof
sections.b:
(1) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the rules and standing orders regulating the procedure of Parliament, there shall be freedom of speech in Parliament. (2) No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof, and no person shall be so liable in respect of the publication by or under the authority of either House of Parliament of any report, paper, votes or proceedings. 1[(3) In other respects, the powers, privileges and immunities of each House of Parliament, and of the members and the committees of each House, shall be such as may from time to time be defined by Parliament by law, and, until so defined, 2[shall be those of that House and of its members and committees immediately before the coming into force of section 15 of the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978.]]. notified). (4) The provisions of clauses (1), (2) and (3) shall apply in relation to persons who by virtue of this Constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of, a House of Parliament or any committee thereof as they apply in relation to members of Parliament.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 21 (date to be 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 15, for certain words This amendment was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 45 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).]
sections.cm:
Members have freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution and the rules of the House.

No member can be taken to any court for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or its committees. Nobody is liable for publishing proceedings under the authority of a House.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The immunity is wide, and for a time it was too wide. In P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) the Court held that it protected MPs who took bribes to vote.

In Sita Soren (2024) a seven-judge bench overruled that ruling. A legislator who takes a bribe can now be prosecuted, whatever Article 105 says about votes in the House.

cl.name: P.V. Narasimha Rao v. State (CBI/SPE)
cl.facts: MPs were alleged to have taken bribes to vote against a no-confidence motion in 1993. They claimed immunity under Article 105(2) for 'anything said or any vote given' in Parliament.
cl.held: By 3–2, MPs who took the bribe AND voted as agreed were immune, because prosecuting them would require questioning the vote. One MP who took money but did not vote got no immunity — an outcome the dissent called an absurdity.
cl.why: It stood for 26 years and was unanimously overruled by a seven-judge bench in Sita Soren (2024).

cl.name: Sita Soren v. Union of India
cl.facts: A Jharkhand MLA was accused of taking a bribe to vote in a Rajya Sabha election, and claimed immunity under Article 194(2) on the authority of Narasimha Rao.
cl.held: Unanimously overruling Narasimha Rao. Immunity attaches only to what is necessary for a legislator to function freely; bribery is complete the moment the money is taken, regardless of how the person later votes, so it is not protected.
cl.why: It ended the anomaly by which taking a bribe and honouring it was immune while taking a bribe and reneging was not.

cl.name: Raja Ram Pal v. Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha
cl.facts: Eleven MPs were expelled after a sting operation showed them accepting money to ask questions. They argued the House had no power to expel, and that courts could not review it in any event.
cl.held: Parliament has the power to expel a member as part of its privileges. But the exercise of that power is subject to judicial review on limited grounds — illegality, unconstitutionality, or violation of natural justice. The expulsions were upheld.
cl.why: It settled that Article 122's bar on questioning proceedings covers procedural irregularity, not substantive illegality.

sections.t: Salaries and allowances of members
sections.b: Members of either House of Parliament shall be entitled to receive such salaries and allowances as may from time to time be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that respect is so made, allowances at such rates and upon such conditions as were immediately before the commencement of this Constitution applicable in the case of members of the Constituent Assembly of the Dominion of India.
sections.cm:
Members' salaries and allowances are whatever Parliament fixes by law.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Parliament sets its own pay, with no outside body involved, and critics have long objected to that. The law is the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954.

sections.t: Provisions as to introduction and passing of Bills
sections.b: (1) Subject to the provisions of articles 109 and 117 with respect to Money Bills and other financial Bills, a Bill may originate in either House of Parliament. (2) Subject to the provisions of articles 108 and 109, a Bill shall not be deemed to have been passed by the Houses of Parliament unless it has been agreed to by both Houses, either without amendment or with such amendments only as are agreed to by both Houses. (3) A Bill pending in Parliament shall not lapse by reason of the prorogation of the Houses. (4) A Bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People shall not lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People. (5) A Bill which is pending in the House of the People, or which having been passed by the House of the People is pending in the Council of States, shall, subject to the provisions of article 108, lapse on a dissolution of the House of the People.
sections.cm:
An ordinary Bill may start in either House, and must be passed by both.

A Bill does not lapse when Parliament is prorogued. A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses when the Lok Sabha is dissolved.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
But a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha has not yet passed does not lapse. The Rajya Sabha is never dissolved, so the Bill survives there.

sections.t: Joint sitting of both Houses in certain cases
sections.b: (1) If after a Bill has been passed by one House and transmitted to the other House— (a) the Bill is rejected by the other House; or (b) the Houses have finally disagreed as to the amendments to be made in the Bill; or (c) more than six months elapse from the date of the reception of the Bill by the other House without the Bill being passed by it, the President may, unless the Bill has elapsed by reason of a dissolution of the House of the People, notify to the Houses by message if they are sitting or by public notification if they are not sitting, his intention to summon them to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose of deliberating and voting on the Bill: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to a Money Bill. (2) In reckoning any such period of six months as is referred to in clause (1), no account shall be taken of any period during which the House referred to in sub-clause (c) of that clause is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days. (3) Where the President has under clause (1) notified his intention of summoning the Houses to meet in a joint sitting, neither House shall proceed further with the Bill, but the President may at any time after the date of his notification summon the Houses to meet in a joint sitting for the purpose specified in the notification and, if he does so, the Houses shall meet accordingly. (4) If at the joint sitting of the two Houses the Bill, with such amendments, if any, as are agreed to in joint sitting, is passed by a majority of the total number of members of both Houses present and voting, it shall be deemed for the purposes of this Constitution to have been passed by both Houses: Provided that at a joint sitting— (a) if the Bill, having been passed by one House, has not been passed by the other House with amendments and returned to the House in which it originated, no amendment shall be proposed to the Bill other than such amendments (if any) as are made necessary by the delay in the passage of the Bill; (b) if the Bill has been so passed and returned, only such amendments as aforesaid shall be proposed to the Bill and such other amendments as are relevant to the matters with respect to which the Houses have not agreed, and the decision of the person presiding as to the amendments which are admissible under this clause shall be final. (5) A joint sitting may be held under this article and a Bill passed thereat, notwithstanding that a dissolution of the House of the People has intervened since the President notified his intention to summon the Houses to meet therein.
sections.cm:
If the two Houses disagree on an ordinary Bill, the President may call a joint sitting. The trigger is that one House rejects the Bill, the Houses disagree on amendments, or six months pass without the second House passing it.

The joint sitting decides by a majority of members present and voting.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Lok Sabha is more than twice the size of the Rajya Sabha. So a joint sitting usually goes the Lok Sabha's way.

A joint sitting is not available for a Money Bill or a Constitution Amendment Bill. Joint sittings have been held only three times, in 1961, 1978 and 2002.

sections.t: Special procedure in respect of Money Bills
sections.b: (1) A Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States. (2) After a Money Bill has been passed by the House of the People it shall be transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations and the Council of States shall within a period of fourteen days from the date of its receipt of the Bill return the Bill to the House of the People with its recommendations and the House of the People may thereupon either accept or reject all or any of the recommendations of the Council of States. (3) If the House of the People accepts any of the recommendations of the Council of States, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses with the amendments recommended by the Council of States and accepted by the House of the People. (4) If the House of the People does not accept any of the recommendations of the Council of States, the Money Bill shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form in which it was passed by the House of the People without any of the amendments recommended by the Council of States. (5) If a Money Bill passed by the House of the People and transmitted to the Council of States for its recommendations is not returned to the House of the People within the said period of fourteen days, it shall be deemed to have been passed by both Houses at the expiration of the said period in the form in which it was passed by the House of the People.
sections.cm:
A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha.

The Rajya Sabha must return it within fourteen days, with or without recommendations. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject the recommendations. Either way, the Bill counts as passed by both Houses.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
If the Rajya Sabha does nothing for fourteen days, the Bill counts as passed anyway. So the Rajya Sabha can neither block a Money Bill nor delay it for long.

No joint sitting is ever needed for a Money Bill, because no deadlock is possible.

sections.t: Definition of “Money Bills”
sections.b: (1) For the purposes of this Chapter, a Bill shall be deemed to be a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with all or any of the following matters, namely:— (a) the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax; (b) the regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government of India, or the amendment of the law with respect to any financial obligations undertaken or to be undertaken by the Government of India; (c) the custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of moneys into or the withdrawal of moneys from any such Fund; (d) the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India; (e) the declaring of any expenditure to be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the increasing of the amount of any such expenditure; (f) the receipt of money on account of the Consolidated Fund of India or the public account of India or the custody or issue of such money or the audit of the accounts of the Union or of a State; or (g) any matter incidental to any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f). (2) A Bill shall not be deemed to be a Money Bill by reason only that it provides for the imposition of fines or other pecuniary penalties, or for the demand or payment of fees for licences or fees for services rendered, or by reason that it provides for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax by any local authority or body for local purposes. (3) If any question arises whether a Bill is a Money Bill or not, the decision of the Speaker of the House of the People thereon shall be final. (4) There shall be endorsed on every Money Bill when it is transmitted to the Council of States under article 109, and when it is presented to the President for assent under article 111, the certificate of the Speaker of the House of the People signed by him that it is a Money Bill.
sections.cm:
A Money Bill is a Bill that deals only with certain money matters. They are taxes, government borrowing, the Consolidated and Contingency Funds, spending from them, and the receipt, custody and audit of public money, plus matters incidental to these.

The Speaker's decision that a Bill is a Money Bill is final.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Two words carry the weight, "only" and "final". One provision outside the list takes a Bill out of the category. But the Speaker's word on the question is final.

The Aadhaar Act, 2016 and the Finance Act, 2017 were passed as Money Bills, so the Rajya Sabha could not reject or amend them. In Rojer Mathew (2019) the Court sent the question of reviewing the Speaker's certificate to a larger bench, which has not yet decided it.

cl.name: Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank Ltd.
cl.facts: Part XIV of the Finance Act, 2017 reorganised tribunals across the country. It had been passed as a Money Bill, which meant the Rajya Sabha could not amend it.
cl.held: The tribunal rules were struck down for compromising judicial independence. On the Money Bill question, the Court held the reasoning in the Aadhaar judgment did not substantially discuss the point, and referred the scope of Article 110 and the reviewability of the Speaker's certificate to a larger bench.
cl.why: The reference on Money Bills is still pending. Until it is decided, whether the Speaker's certificate can be questioned in court remains genuinely open.

cl.name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar)
cl.facts: The Aadhaar Act had been passed as a Money Bill. Its validity, and the legitimacy of that route, were both challenged.
cl.held: By 4–1, Aadhaar was largely upheld and the Money Bill certification was accepted. Justice Chandrachud dissented, holding the certification a fraud on the Constitution and the whole Act void on that ground alone.
cl.why: The majority's Money Bill reasoning is the very holding Rojer Mathew declined to follow and referred to a larger bench.

sections.t: Assent to Bills
sections.b: When a Bill has been passed by the Houses of Parliament, it shall be presented to the President, and the President shall declare either that he assents to the Bill, or that he withholds assent therefrom: Provided that the President may, as soon as possible after the presentation to him of a Bill for assent, return the Bill if it is not a Money Bill to the Houses with a message requesting that they will reconsider the Bill or any specified provisions thereof and, in particular, will consider the desirability of introducing any such amendments as he may recommend in his message, and when a Bill is so returned, the Houses shall reconsider the Bill accordingly, and if the Bill is passed again by the Houses with or without amendment and presented to the President for assent, the President shall not withhold assent therefrom.
sections.cm:
When a Bill passed by Parliament reaches the President, the President may assent or withhold assent. For a Bill that is not a Money Bill, the President may instead return it for reconsideration.

If both Houses pass the Bill again, with or without changes, the President must assent.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The article sets no time limit, either for the first decision or after reconsideration. So a President can simply sit on a Bill, which is called the pocket veto.

President Zail Singh did so with the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986, which would have allowed the interception of post. The Bill never became law.

sections.t: Annual financial statement
sections.b: (1) The President shall in respect of every financial year cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year, in this Part referred to as the "annual financial statement''. (2) The estimates of expenditure embodied in the annual financial statement shall show separately— (a) the sums required to meet expenditure described by this Constitution as expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India; and (b) the sums required to meet other expenditure proposed to be made from the Consolidated Fund of India, and shall distinguish expenditure on revenue account from other expenditure. (3) The following expenditure shall be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India— (a) the emoluments and allowances of the President and other expenditure relating to his office; (b) the salaries and allowances of the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People; (c) debt charges for which the Government of India is liable including interest, sinking fund charges and redemption charges, and other expenditure relating to the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt; (d) (i) the salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Supreme Court; (ii) the pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of the Federal Court; (iii) the pensions payable to or in respect of Judges of any High Court which exercises jurisdiction in relation to any area included in the territory of India or which at any time before the commencement of this Constitution exercised jurisdiction in relation to any area included in 1[a Governor's Province of the Dominion of India]; (e) the salary, allowances and pension payable to or in respect of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India; (f) any sums required to satisfy any judgment, decree or award of any court or arbitral tribunal; (g) any other expenditure declared by this Constitution or by Parliament by law to be so charged.
sections.cm:
Every financial year, the President lays an annual financial statement before both Houses. The statement is the Budget.

The statement shows the government's estimated receipts and spending. Spending charged on the Consolidated Fund is shown apart from other spending.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Charged spending can be discussed in Parliament, but not voted on. The charged items include the President's pay, the salaries of Supreme Court judges, debt charges and the salary of the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

So a hostile majority cannot starve these offices of money by refusing a demand.

sections.t: Procedure in Parliament with respect to estimates
sections.b:
(1) So much of the estimates as relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament, but nothing in this clause shall be construed as preventing the discussion in either House of Parliament of any of those estimates. "a Province corresponding to a State specified in Part A of the First Schedule" (2) So much of the said estimates as relates to other expenditure shall be submitted in the form of demands for grants to the House of the People, and the House of the People shall have power to assent, or to refuse to assent, to any demand, or to assent to any demand subject to a reduction of the amount specified therein. (3) No demand for a grant shall be made except on the recommendation of the President.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch., for "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule".]
sections.cm:
Charged spending is not put to the vote of Parliament. Other spending goes to the Lok Sabha as demands for grants, which it may accept, refuse or reduce. A demand can be moved only on the President's recommendation.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Cut motions are the opposition's main tool at this stage. There are three kinds: a policy cut, an economy cut and a token cut.

In practice most demands are never discussed. The Speaker applies the guillotine, and all the remaining demands are put to the vote together.

sections.t: Appropriation Bills
sections.b: (1) As soon as may be after the grants under article 113 have been made by the House of the People, there shall be introduced a Bill to provide for the appropriation out of the Consolidated Fund of India of all moneys required to meet— (a) the grants so made by the House of the People; and (b) the expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India but not exceeding in any case the amount shown in the statement previously laid before Parliament. (2) No amendment shall be proposed to any such Bill in either House of Parliament which will have the effect of varying the amount or altering the destination of any grant so made or of varying the amount of any expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, and the decision of the person presiding as to whether an amendment is inadmissible under this clause shall be final. (3) Subject to the provisions of articles 115 and 116, no money shall be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by law passed in accordance with the provisions of this article.
sections.cm:
After the Lok Sabha passes the demands, an Appropriation Bill authorises the government to draw the money from the Consolidated Fund.

No amendment may change the amount or purpose of a grant. And no money may be drawn except under an Appropriation Act.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 114 is the constitutional lock on the treasury. Money leaves the Consolidated Fund only when the legislature has authorised it.

sections.t: Supplementary, additional or excess grants
sections.b: (1) The President shall— (a) if the amount authorised by any law made in accordance with the provisions of article 114 to be expended for a particular service for the current financial year is found to be insufficient for the purposes of that year or when a need has arisen during the current financial year for supplementary or additional expenditure upon some new service not contemplated in the annual financial statement for that year; or (b) if any money has been spent on any service during a financial year in excess of the amount granted for that service and for that year, cause to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament another statement showing the estimated amount of that expenditure or cause to be presented to the House of the People a demand for such excess, as the case may be. (2) The provisions of articles 112, 113 and 114 shall have effect in relation to any such statement and expenditure or demand and also to any law to be made authorising the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India to meet such expenditure or the grant in respect of such demand as they have effect in relation to the annual financial statement and the expenditure mentioned therein or to a demand for a grant and the law to be made for the authorisation of appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India to meet such expenditure or grant.
sections.cm:
Supplementary, additional and excess grants cover spending beyond what the Budget authorised. They follow the same procedure as the Budget.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
An excess grant is approved only after the Public Accounts Committee has examined it. So excess grants are the one case where money is spent first and sanctioned later.

sections.t: Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
sections.b: (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Chapter, the House of the People shall have power— (a) to make any grant in advance in respect of the estimated expenditure for a part of any financial year pending the completion of the procedure prescribed in article 113 for the voting of such grant and the passing of the law in accordance with the provisions of article 114 in relation to that expenditure; (b) to make a grant for meeting an unexpected demand upon the resources of India when on account of the magnitude or the indefinite character of the service the demand cannot be stated with the details ordinarily given in an annual financial statement; (c) to make an exceptional grant which forms no part of the current service of any financial year, and Parliament shall have power to authorise by law the withdrawal of moneys from the Consolidated Fund of India for the purposes for which the said grants are made. (2) The provisions of articles 113 and 114 shall have effect in relation to the making of any grant under clause (1) and to any law to be made under that clause as they have effect in relation to the making of a grant with regard to any expenditure mentioned in the annual financial statement and the law to be made for the authorisation of appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India to meet such expenditure.
sections.cm:
Article 116 provides three devices. A vote on account gives money in advance before the Budget passes. A vote of credit meets a large or open-ended need that cannot be stated in detail. An exceptional grant covers spending outside any current service.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A vote on account normally covers two months. In an election year it covers longer, and the government presents what is popularly called an interim budget. The interim budget works through Article 116, not through a separate device.

sections.t: Special provisions as to financial Bills
sections.b: (1) A Bill or amendment making provision for any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f) of clause (1) of article 110 shall not be introduced or moved except on the recommendation of the President and a Bill making such provision shall not be introduced in the Council of States: Provided that no recommendation shall be required under this clause for the moving of an amendment making provision for the reduction or abolition of any tax. (2) A Bill or amendment shall not be deemed to make provision for any of the matters aforesaid by reason only that it provides for the imposition of fines or other pecuniary penalties, or for the demand or payment of fees for licences or fees for services rendered, or by reason that it provides for the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax by any local authority or body for local purposes. (3) A Bill which, if enacted and brought into operation, would involve expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India shall not be passed by either House of Parliament unless the President has recommended to that House the consideration of the Bill.
sections.cm:
A Bill that includes any matter listed in Article 110, along with other provisions, needs the President's recommendation to be introduced, and cannot start in the Rajya Sabha.

A Bill that would involve spending from the Consolidated Fund needs the President's recommendation before either House considers it.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A Bill of either kind is a Financial Bill, not a Money Bill. So the Rajya Sabha keeps its full powers over it, even where the Bill could not start there.

sections.t: Rules of procedure
sections.b: (1) Each House of Parliament may make rules for regulating, subject to the provisions of this Constitution, its procedure* and the conduct of its business. (2) Until rules are made under clause (1), the rules of procedure and standing orders in force immediately before the commencement of this Constitution with respect to the Legislature of the Dominion of India shall have effect in relation to Parliament subject to such modifications and adaptations as may be made therein by the Chairman of the Council of States or the Speaker of the House of the People, as the case may be. (3) The President, after consultation with the Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker of the House of the People, may make rules as to the procedure with respect to joint sittings of, and communications between, the two Houses. (4) At a joint sitting of the two Houses the Speaker of the House of the People, or in his absence such person as may be determined by rules of procedure made under clause (3), shall preside.
sections.cm:
Each House may make rules for its own procedure and business. Until it does, the rules from before the Constitution apply. The President makes the rules for joint sittings, after consulting the presiding officers.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The rules, not the Constitution, govern Question Hour, Zero Hour and whether a Bill goes to a committee at all. Under Article 122 the presiding officer's reading of the rules is final.

sections.t: Regulation by law of procedure in Parliament in relation to financial business
sections.b:
Parliament may, for the purpose of the timely completion of financial business, regulate by law the procedure of, and the conduct of business in, each House of Parliament in relation to any financial matter or to any Bill for the appropriation of moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India, and, if and so far as any provision of any law so made is inconsistent with any rule made by a House of Parliament under clause (1) of article 118 or with any rule or standing order having effect in relation to Parliament under clause (2) of that article, such provision shall prevail.

[Editorial Notes: * The brackets and words "(including the quorum to constitute a meeting of the House" ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 22 (date not notified). This amendment was omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 45 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).]
sections.cm:
Parliament may make a law on financial procedure and on finishing financial business on time. The law would override the Houses' own rules.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Parliament has never made such a law. Financial procedure runs entirely on the Houses' own rules, which the Houses can change themselves.

sections.t: Language to be used in Parliament
sections.b: (1) Notwithstanding anything in Part XVII, but subject to the provisions of article 348, business in Parliament shall be transacted in Hindi or in English: Provided that the Chairman of the Council of States or Speaker of the House of the People, or person acting as such, as the case may be, may permit any member who cannot adequately express himself in Hindi or in English to address the House in his mother-tongue. (2) Unless Parliament by law otherwise provides, this article shall, after the expiration of a period of fifteen years from the commencement of this Constitution, have effect as if the words “or in English” were omitted therefrom.
sections.cm:
Parliament does its business in Hindi or English. The presiding officer may let a member who cannot speak well in either use their mother tongue.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The use of English was to end after fifteen years, unless Parliament decided otherwise. Parliament did, and English continues indefinitely under the Official Languages Act, 1963.

sections.t: Restriction on discussion in Parliament
