sections.b: No discussion shall take place in Parliament with respect to the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in the discharge of his duties except upon a motion for presenting an address to the President praying for the removal of the Judge as hereinafter provided.
sections.cm:
Parliament may not discuss the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in carrying out judicial duties. The only exception is a motion to remove the judge.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 121 shields judges from criticism in Parliament. A motion for removal is the only occasion on which a judge's conduct may be debated there.

sections.t: Courts not to inquire into proceedings of Parliament
sections.b: (1) The validity of any proceedings in Parliament shall not be called in question on the ground of any alleged irregularity of procedure. (2) No officer or member of Parliament in whom powers are vested by or under this Constitution for regulating procedure or the conduct of business, or for maintaining order, in Parliament shall be subject to the jurisdiction of any court in respect of the exercise by him of those powers.
sections.cm:
No court may question the validity of proceedings in Parliament on the ground of an irregularity of procedure. Nor can a court act against an officer of Parliament for using powers to regulate procedure.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
But an irregularity is not the same as an illegality. Courts have held that they may still step in where a proceeding is unconstitutional, not merely irregular.

So the Speaker's certificate that a Bill is a Money Bill came to be argued as open to review.

sections.t: Power of President to promulgate Ordinances during recess of Parliament
sections.ct: THE UNION - LEGISLATIVE POWERS OF THE PRESIDENT
sections.b: (1) If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require. (2) An Ordinance promulgated under this article shall have the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but every such Ordinance— (a) shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament and shall cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or, if before the expiration of that period resolutions disapproving it are passed by both Houses, upon the passing of the second of those resolutions; and (b) may be withdrawn at any time by the President. Explanation.—Where the Houses of Parliament are summoned to reassemble on different dates, the period of six weeks shall be reckoned from the later of those dates for the purposes of this clause. (3) If and so far as an Ordinance under this article makes any provision which Parliament would not under this Constitution be competent to enact, it shall be void. 1(4)* * * * *
sections.cm:
Unless both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President may make an ordinance when immediate action is needed. An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament.

The ordinance must be laid before both Houses. The ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or sooner if both Houses disapprove it.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The satisfaction is really the Council of Ministers' satisfaction, not the President's own. And the courts can review it.

Governments have abused the power. Bihar kept re-making the same ordinances for years without putting them to the legislature, and D.C. Wadhwa (1987) called that a fraud on the Constitution. Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that laying an ordinance before the legislature is mandatory, and that re-promulgation to keep a law alive is unconstitutional.

cl.name: D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar
cl.facts: A professor documented that Bihar had promulgated 256 ordinances between 1967 and 1981, re-promulgating many of them again and again — some kept alive for as long as fourteen years without ever being put to the legislature.
cl.held: Re-promulgation of ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a 'fraud on the Constitution' and a subversion of the democratic process. The executive cannot usurp the legislature's function.
cl.why: The foundational case against ordinance raj, and the reason ordinance re-promulgation is now legally suspect rather than merely criticised.

cl.name: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
cl.facts: Bihar took over Sanskrit schools by an ordinance that was re-promulgated seven times and never enacted. Teachers claimed their employment survived.
cl.held: Re-promulgation is unconstitutional. An ordinance that lapses does not create enduring rights unless irreversibility or public interest demands it. And the satisfaction of the President or Governor in issuing one is not immune from judicial review.
cl.why: It removed the last shelter for serial ordinances and confirmed that the 38th Amendment's attempt to make that satisfaction final did not survive the 44th.

sections.t: Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court
sections.b:
(1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than *[seven] other Judges. (2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal 2[on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission referred to in article 124A] and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years: 3[* * * * *] 4[Provided that]— (a) a Judge may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office; (b) a Judge may be removed from his office in the manner provided in clause (4). (3) A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court unless he is a citizen of India and— (a) has been for at least five years a Judge of a High Court or of two or more such Courts in succession; or (b) has been for at least ten years an advocate of a High Court or of two or more such Courts in succession; or (c) is, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist. Explanation I.—In this clause "High Court'' means a High Court which exercises, or which at any time before the commencement of this Constitution exercised, jurisdiction in any part of the territory of India. Explanation II.—In computing for the purpose of this clause the period during which a person has been an advocate, any period during which a person has held judicial office not inferior to that of a district judge after he became an advocate shall be included. (4) A Judge of the Supreme Court shall not be removed from his office except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. (5) Parliament may by law regulate the procedure for the presentation of an address and for the investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or incapacity of a Judge under clause (4). (6) Every person appointed to be a Judge of the Supreme Court shall, before he enters upon his office, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule. (7) No person who has held office as a Judge of the Supreme Court shall plead or act in any court or before any authority within the territory of India.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Thirty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1975, s. 2 (with retrospective effect) and 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014, s. 2, for "after consultation with 4. Subs. by s. 2, ibid. for "provided further that" This amendment has been struck down by the Supreme omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 16 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). * Now “thirty-three” vide the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019 (37 of 2019), s. 2 (w.e.f. 9-8-2019). such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Court in the States as the President may deem necessary for the purpose" (w.e.f. 13-4-2015). This amendment has been struck down by the Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and another Vs. Union of India in its judgment dated 16-10-2015, AIR 2016 SC 117. 3. The first proviso was omitted by s. 2, ibid. The proviso was as under:— "Provided that in the case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of India shall always be consulted:" This amendment has been struck down by the Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and another Vs. Union of India in its judgment dated 16-10-2015, AIR 2016 SC 117. Court in the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and another Vs Union of India judgment dated 16-10-2015, AIR 2016 SC 117. 1[(2A) The age of a Judge of the Supreme Court shall be determined by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law provide.]]
sections.cm:
Article 124 sets up the Supreme Court. The Court has a Chief Justice and as many other judges as Parliament fixes by law.

The President appoints the judges after consulting the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts that the President thinks necessary. A judge serves until 65. A judge can be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by an address of both Houses.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The text says "consultation". But the Second Judges case (1993) and the Third Judges case (1998) read it as "concurrence". They created a collegium of the Chief Justice and the four senior-most judges, which in effect chooses the judges.

The 99th Amendment (2014) tried to replace the collegium with a National Judicial Appointments Commission. In 2015 the Court struck the amendment down, holding that judicial primacy in appointments is part of the basic structure. So the system that actually appoints judges appears nowhere in Article 124.

cl.name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India
cl.facts: The First Judges Case had given the executive primacy in appointing judges. Twelve years later the Court was asked to reconsider.
cl.held: 'Consultation' with the Chief Justice of India means concurrence. The Chief Justice's opinion, formed after consulting senior colleagues, has primacy — creating the collegium.
cl.why: It invented the collegium system, which is nowhere in the text of Article 124, and which has governed judicial appointments ever since.

cl.name: In Re: Special Reference No. 1 of 1998
cl.facts: The President made a reference under Article 143 asking the Court to clarify the consultation process after a disputed set of recommendations.
cl.held: The collegium for Supreme Court appointments is the Chief Justice plus the four senior-most judges; for High Court appointments, the Chief Justice plus two. A recommendation made without this consultation is not binding on the government.
cl.why: It fixed the collegium's composition and procedure in the form still used today.

cl.name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India
cl.facts: The 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act replaced the collegium with a six-member commission: the Chief Justice, the two next senior judges, the Law Minister and two eminent persons. Any two members could block a recommendation — so the Law Minister and one eminent person together could veto a name.
cl.held: By 4–1, both struck down. Judicial primacy in appointments is part of the independence of the judiciary, which is part of the basic structure. The presence of the Law Minister and the veto to lay members compromised it.
cl.why: The most recent successful basic-structure challenge, and the reason the collegium — which the Court itself created — remains in place.

sections.t: National Judicial Appointments Commission
sections.b:
(1) There shall be a Commission to be known as the National Judicial Appointments Commission consisting of the following, namely:— amendment (2) No act or proceedings of the National Judicial Appointments Commission shall be questioned or be invalidated merely on the ground of the existence of any vacancy or defect in the constitution of the Commission.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, s. 2 (w.e.f. 5-10-1963). 2. Ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014, s. 3 (w.e.f. 13-4-2015). This has been struck down by the Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates- on-Record Association and another Vs Union of India in its judgment dated 16-10-2015, AIR 2016 SC 117. (a) the Chief Justice of India, Chairperson, ex officio; (b) two other senior Judges of the Supreme Court next to the Chief Justice of India--Members, ex officio; (c) the Union Minister in charge of Law and Justice--Member, ex officio; (d) two eminent persons to be nominated by the committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Chief Justice of India and the Leader of Opposition in the House of the People or where there is no such Leader of Opposition, then, the Leader of single largest Opposition Party in the House of the People--Members: Provided that one of the eminent person shall be nominated from amongst the persons belonging to the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Minorities or Women: Provided further that an eminent person shall be nominated for a period of three years and shall not be eligible for renomination.]
sections.cm:
Article 124A set up the National Judicial Appointments Commission. The members were the Chief Justice, the two next senior judges, the Law Minister and two eminent persons.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 99th Amendment inserted the article in 2014. In 2015 a bench of five judges struck it down by four to one, because it breached judicial independence, which is part of the basic structure.

The article is still printed in the text, but has no legal effect.

sections.t: Functions of Commission
sections.b: It shall be the duty of the National Judicial Appointments Commission to— (a) recommend persons for appointment as Chief Justice of India, Judges of the Supreme Court, Chief Justices of High Courts and other Judges of High Courts; (b) recommend transfer of Chief Justices and other Judges of High Courts from one High Court to any other High Court; and (c) ensure that the person recommended is of ability and integrity.
sections.cm:
Article 124B would have given the Commission the job of recommending appointments and transfers of judges.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Court struck it down with Article 124A in 2015.

sections.t: Power of Parliament to make law
sections.b: Parliament may, by law, regulate the procedure for the appointment of Chief Justice of India and other Judges of the Supreme Court and Chief Justices and other Judges of High Courts and empower the Commission to lay down by regulations the procedure for the discharge of its functions, the manner of selection of persons for appointment and such other matters as may be considered necessary by it.]
sections.cm:
Article 124C would have let Parliament regulate the Commission's procedure by law.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Court struck it down with Articles 124A and 124B in 2015.

sections.t: Salaries, etc., of Judges
sections.b:
1[(1) There shall be paid to the Judges of the Supreme Court such salaries as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such salaries as are specified in the Second Schedule.] (2) Every Judge shall be entitled to such privileges and allowances and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and pension as may from time to time be determined by or under law made by Parliament and, until so determined, to such privileges, allowances and rights as are specified in the Second Schedule: Provided that neither the privileges nor the allowances of a Judge nor his rights in respect of leave of absence or pension shall be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Fifty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1986, s. 2, for cl. (1)]
sections.cm:
Judges' salaries are fixed by Parliament. Their privileges, allowances, leave and pension cannot be changed to their disadvantage after appointment.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The bar on changes for the worse is a core guarantee of judicial independence. The one exception is a financial emergency, when Article 360(4)(b) allows judges' salaries to be cut.

sections.t: Appointment of acting Chief Justice
sections.b: When the office of Chief Justice of India is vacant or when the Chief Justice is, by reason of absence or otherwise, unable to perform the duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by such one of the other Judges of the Court as the President may appoint for the purpose.
sections.cm:
When the Chief Justice's office is vacant, or the Chief Justice cannot act, the President appoints another judge of the Court to act as Chief Justice.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The President appoints, but by convention the senior-most judge acts.

Do not confuse acting with appointment. The supersessions of 1973 and 1977, when senior judges were passed over, concerned the permanent appointment of a Chief Justice under Article 124.

sections.t: Appointment of ad hoc Judges
sections.b: (1) If at any time there should not be a quorum of the Judges of the Supreme Court available to hold or continue any session of the Court, 1[the National Judicial Appointments Commission on a reference made to it by the Chief Justice of India, may with the previous consent of the President] and after consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, request in writing the attendance at the sittings of the Court, as an ad hoc Judge, for such period as may be necessary, of a Judge of a High Court duly qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court to be designated by the Chief Justice of India. (2) It shall be the duty of the Judge who has been so designated, in priority to other duties of his office, to attend the sittings of the Supreme Court at the time and for the period for which his attendance is required, and while so attending he shall have all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges, and shall discharge the duties, of a Judge of the Supreme Court.
sections.cm:
If there are too few permanent judges to make a quorum, the Chief Justice may ask a qualified High Court judge to sit in the Supreme Court as an ad hoc judge. The Chief Justice needs the President's consent, and must consult the High Court's Chief Justice.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The power is rarely used. When the Court needs extra judges, it is more likely to bring back retired judges under Article 128.

sections.t: Attendance of retired Judges at sittings of the Supreme Court
sections.b:
Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, 2[the National Judicial Appointments Commission] may at any time, with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of a Judge of the Supreme Court or of the Federal Court 3[or who has held the office of a Judge of a High Court and is duly qualified for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court] to sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court, and every such person so requested shall, while so sitting and acting, be entitled to such allowances as the President may by order determine and have all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of, but shall not otherwise be deemed to be, a Judge of that Court: Justice of India may, with the previous consent of the President" Provided that nothing in this article shall be deemed to require any such person as aforesaid to sit and act as a Judge of that Court unless he consents so to do.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014, s. 4, for "the Chief 2. Subs. by s. 5, ibid., for "the Chief Justice of India" (w.e.f. 13-4-2015). This amendment 3. Ins. by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, s. 3 (w.e.f. 5-10-1963). This amendment has been struck down by the Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and another vs. Union of India in its judgment dated 16-10-2015, AIR 2016 SC 117. has been struck down by the Supreme Court in the case of Supreme Court Advocates- on-Record Association and another Vs. Union of India in its judgment dated 16-10- 2015, AIR 2016 SC 117.]
sections.cm:
With the President's consent, the Chief Justice may ask a retired Supreme Court judge, or a qualified retired High Court judge, to sit and act as a Supreme Court judge.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The retired judge must also agree. Nobody can be compelled back to the bench.

sections.t: Supreme Court to be a court of record
sections.b: The Supreme Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish for contempt of itself.
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court is a court of record, with all the powers of such a court. The powers include punishing anyone for contempt of the Court.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Being a court of record does two things. The Court's records and judgments are kept permanently as evidence, and cannot be questioned in any court. And the power to punish for contempt comes from the Constitution itself.

So the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 only regulates the power, and its limits do not confine the Court. Parliament can set the procedure, but cannot take the power away.

sections.t: Seat of Supreme Court
sections.b: The Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places, as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from time to time, appoint.
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court sits in Delhi, or in any other place the Chief Justice names with the President's approval.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Proposals for permanent regional benches keep coming up under Article 130. The Court has consistently resisted splitting itself.

sections.t: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
sections.b: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the Supreme Court shall, to the exclusion of any other court, have original jurisdiction in any dispute— (a) between the Government of India and one or more States; or (b) between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other; or (c) between two or more States, if and in so far as the dispute involves any question (whether of law or fact) on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends: 1[Provided that the said jurisdiction shall not extend to a dispute arising out of any treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument which, having been entered into or executed before the commencement of this Constitution, continues in operation after such commencement, or which provides that the said jurisdiction shall not extend to such a dispute.]
sections.cm:
Only the Supreme Court can hear disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between States. The dispute must turn on a question of law or fact on which a legal right depends.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The dispute must be about a legal right, not a political grievance. Some suits by States against the Union have been resisted on that ground.

The forum is narrow in other ways too. Private parties cannot use it, disputes under treaties made before the Constitution are excluded, and Parliament has taken inter-State water disputes out of the courts under Article 262.

cl.name: State of Karnataka v. Union of India
cl.short: State of Karnataka v. Union of India
cl.facts: The Centre appointed a commission of inquiry into allegations against Karnataka's Chief Minister and ministers. The State sued the Union directly under Article 131.
cl.held: A suit under Article 131 lies wherever a legal right of a State against the Union is in issue, and the State need not show a cause of action in the ordinary civil sense. The dispute must be legal, though, not merely political.
cl.why: The leading case on when a State may sue the Centre in the Supreme Court's exclusive original jurisdiction, revived by Kerala's borrowing-limits suit and Chhattisgarh's challenge to the NIA Act.

sections.t: Exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in regard to questions as to constitutional validity of Central laws
sections.b: Omitted.
sections.cm:
Article 131A gave the Supreme Court sole power to decide whether central laws were constitutional.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment inserted it, and the 43rd repealed it in 1977. The article was one of the changes that had taken judicial review away from the High Courts.

sections.t: Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in certain cases
sections.b:
(1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree or final order of a High Court in the territory of India, whether in a civil, criminal or other proceeding, 3[if the High Court certifies under article 134A] that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution. Court certifies" 1(2)* * * * * (3) Where such a certificate is given, 2*** any party in the case may appeal to the Supreme Court on the ground that any such question as aforesaid has been wrongly decided 2***. Explanation.—For the purposes of this article, the expression “final order” includes an order deciding an issue which, if decided in favour of the appellant, would be sufficient for the final disposal of the case.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 5, for the proviso 2. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 23 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977). 3. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 17, for "if the High]
sections.cm:
An appeal lies to the Supreme Court from any judgment of a High Court, civil, criminal or other. The High Court must certify that the case raises a substantial question of law on the meaning of the Constitution.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The certificate route is now rarely used. Almost every constitutional case reaches the Supreme Court by special leave under Article 136, which needs no certificate.

sections.t: Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in appeals from High Courts in regard to civil matters
sections.b: 3[(1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, decree or final order in a civil proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India 4[if the High Court certifies under article 134A—] (a) that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance; and (b) that in the opinion of the High Court the said question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.] (2) Notwithstanding anything in article 132, any party appealing to the Supreme Court under clause (1) may urge as one of the grounds in such appeal that a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution has been wrongly decided. (3) Notwithstanding anything in this article, no appeal shall, unless Parliament by law otherwise provides, lie to the Supreme Court from the judgment, decree or final order of one Judge of a High Court.
sections.cm:
An appeal lies in a civil case where the High Court certifies two things. The case must raise a substantial question of law of general importance, and the High Court must think the Supreme Court needs to decide it.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 30th Amendment (1972) removed the old test of a dispute worth ₹20,000 or more. Importance replaced money as the test.

sections.t: Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in regard to criminal matters
sections.b:
(1) An appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court from any judgment, final order or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India if the High Court— (a) has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to death; or (b) has withdrawn for trial before itself any case from any court subordinate to its authority and has in such trial convicted the accused person and sentenced him to death; or (c) 5[certifies under article 134A] that the case is a fit one for appeal to the Supreme Court: (2) Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court any further powers to entertain and hear appeals from any judgment, final order or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India subject to such conditions and limitations as may be specified in such law.

[Editorial Notes: 3. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirtieth Amendment) Act, 1972, s. 2, for cl. (1) 4. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s.18, for "if the High 5. Subs. by s. 19, ibid., for "certifies" (w.e.f. 1-8-1979). 1. Cl. (2) omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 17, for "if the High Court certifies" (w.e.f. 1-8-1979). 2. Certain words omitted by s. 17, ibid. (w.e.f. 1-8-1979). (w.e.f. 27-2-1973). Court certifies.—" (w.e.f. 1-8-1979). Provided that an appeal under sub-clause (c) shall lie subject to such provisions as may be made in that behalf under clause (1) of article 145 and to such conditions as the High Court may establish or require.]
sections.cm:
An appeal lies as of right in a criminal case in three situations. The High Court has reversed an acquittal and passed a death sentence. Or the High Court has taken a case to itself and passed a death sentence. Or the High Court certifies the case as fit for appeal.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A death sentence makes the appeal automatic. Anything less needs a certificate, or special leave under Article 136.

sections.t: Certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court
sections.b: Every High Court, passing or making a judgment, decree, final order, or sentence, referred to in clause (1) of article 132 or clause (1) of article 133, or clause (1) of article 134,— (a) may, if it deems fit so to do, on its own motion; and (b) shall, if an oral application is made, by or on behalf of the party aggrieved, immediately after the passing or making of such judgment, decree, final order or sentence, determine, as soon as may be after such passing or making, the question whether a certificate of the nature referred to in clause (1) of article 132, or clause (1) of article 133 or, as the case may be, sub-clause (c) of clause (1) of article 134, may be given in respect of that case.]
sections.cm:
A High Court must decide whether to grant a certificate for appeal under Article 132, 133 or 134. The High Court does so on its own, or when a party asks orally right after the judgment.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 44th Amendment added the article, so that litigants no longer had to file a separate application later.

sections.t: Jurisdiction and powers of the Federal Court under existing law to be exercisable by the Supreme Court
sections.b: Until Parliament by law otherwise provides, the Supreme Court shall also have jurisdiction and powers with respect to any matter to which the provisions of article 133 or article 134 do not apply if jurisdiction and powers in relation to that matter were exercisable by the Federal Court immediately before the commencement of this Constitution under any existing law.
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court takes over any jurisdiction that the Federal Court had under laws made before the Constitution, unless Parliament provides otherwise.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The article is largely spent. Article 135 matters only for a few pre-1950 statutory jurisdictions that were never re-enacted.

sections.t: Special leave to appeal by the Supreme Court
sections.b: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the Supreme Court may, in its discretion, grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India. (2) Nothing in clause (1) shall apply to any judgment, determination, sentence or order passed or made by any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court may, at its discretion, allow an appeal against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal in India. Courts martial and other armed forces tribunals are the only exception.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Special leave is a discretion, not a right. No litigant can demand it, and the Court gives no reasons for refusing. The Court has said it will use the power sparingly, in exceptional cases.

But in practice the special leave petition has become the main route into the Supreme Court. Most of the Court's docket comes through it.

cl.name: Pritam Singh v. The State
cl.facts: One of the first special leave petitions filed under the new Constitution asked the Court to define when it would grant leave.
cl.held: Article 136 confers a wide discretionary power to be exercised sparingly and in exceptional cases only, where a substantial question of law or grave injustice is shown. It is not a regular avenue of appeal.
cl.why: The standard the Court still recites — and, given that special leave now supplies most of its docket, the standard most often honoured in the breach.

sections.t: Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court
sections.b:
Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under article 145, the Supreme Court shall have power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 20 (w.e.f. 1-8-1979).]
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court may review any judgment or order it has given, subject to any law of Parliament and to the Court's own rules under Article 145.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
A review is not a fresh hearing. The grounds are narrow: new and important evidence, an error plain on the face of the record, or another sufficient reason. Disagreeing with the result is not enough.

When a review fails, one more remedy remains. In Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002) the Court created the curative petition, and rested it on Article 142, not on Article 137.

sections.t: Enlargement of the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
sections.b: (1) The Supreme Court shall have such further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any of the matters in the Union List as Parliament may by law confer. (2) The Supreme Court shall have such further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any matter as the Government of India and the Government of any State may by special agreement confer, if Parliament by law provides for the exercise of such jurisdiction and powers by the Supreme Court.
sections.cm:
Parliament may widen the Supreme Court's jurisdiction over Union List matters. Parliament may widen it over other matters too, if the State government agrees.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Both conditions, a law of Parliament and, for other matters, a State's agreement, have kept the power almost unused.

sections.t: Conferment on the Supreme Court of powers to issue certain writs
sections.b: Parliament may by law confer on the Supreme Court power to issue directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for any purposes other than those mentioned in clause (2) of article 32.
sections.cm:
Parliament may by law give the Supreme Court power to issue writs for purposes other than enforcing fundamental rights.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Without such a law, the Court's writ power under Article 32 covers only fundamental rights. But a High Court's power under Article 226 is wider already.

sections.t: Transfer of certain cases
sections.b: 2[(1) Where cases involving the same or substantially the same questions of law are pending before the Supreme Court and one or more High Courts or before two or more High Courts and the Supreme Court is satisfied on its own motion or on an application made by the Attorney-General of India or by a party to any such case that such questions are substantial questions of general importance, the Supreme Court may withdraw the case or cases pending before the High Court or the High Courts and dispose of all the cases itself: Provided that the Supreme Court may after determining the said questions of law return any case so withdrawn together with a copy of its judgment on such questions to the High Court from which the case has been withdrawn, and the High Court shall on receipt thereof, proceed to dispose of the case in conformity with such judgment.] (2) The Supreme Court may, if it deems it expedient so to do for the ends of justice, transfer any case, appeal or other proceedings pending before any High Court to any other High Court.]
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court may take over cases that raise the same substantial question of law, when they are pending before it and one or more High Courts, or before two or more High Courts. The Court may also move any case from one High Court to another.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment added the article, and it has stayed.

The Court uses it to decide a single question once, instead of in many courts. The Court also uses it to move a case when justice requires it.

sections.t: Ancillary powers of the Supreme Court
sections.b:
Parliament may by law make provision for conferring upon the Supreme Court such supplemental powers not inconsistent with any of the provisions of this Constitution as may appear to be necessary or desirable for the purpose of enabling the Court more effectively to exercise the jurisdiction conferred upon it by or under this Constitution.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 24 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977). 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 21, for cl. (1)]
sections.cm:
Parliament may give the Supreme Court extra powers that help it exercise its jurisdiction better, so long as they fit with the Constitution.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Whatever Parliament grants must stay within the Constitution. So Article 140 cannot be used to stretch Article 142 beyond its own limits.

sections.t: Law declared by Supreme Court to be binding on all courts
sections.b: The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
sections.cm:
The law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts in India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
"All courts" means all courts below the Supreme Court. The Court can overrule its own earlier decisions, as it did with ADM Jabalpur and P.V. Narasimha Rao. But only a larger bench can do so. A bench of equal strength that disagrees must refer the question to a larger bench.

Only the ratio binds, meaning the reasoning needed to decide the case. Remarks made in passing, called obiter dicta, persuade at most.

cl.name: Bengal Immunity Co. Ltd. v. State of Bihar
cl.facts: The Court was asked to reconsider its own recent decision on inter-State sales tax.
cl.held: The Supreme Court is not bound by its own previous decisions. It may reconsider and depart from them, particularly in constitutional matters where no correction by legislation is possible.
cl.why: It established that 'all courts' in Article 141 does not include the Supreme Court itself — the basis on which Golak Nath, Kesavananda, Puttaswamy and Sita Soren were all possible.

sections.t: Enforcement of decrees and orders of the Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc
sections.b: (1) The Supreme Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India in such manner as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, in such manner as the President may by order1 prescribe. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made in this behalf by Parliament, the Supreme Court shall, as respects the whole of the territory of India, have all and every power to make any order for the purpose of securing the attendance of any person, the discovery or production of any documents, or the investigation or punishment of any contempt of itself.
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court may pass any decree or order needed to do complete justice in a case before it. The order can be enforced throughout India.

The Court may also require people to attend, order documents to be produced, and punish for contempt.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 142 is the most open-ended power in the Constitution. The Court has used it to settle the Bhopal gas claims in 1989, to order the Ayodhya settlement in 2019, and to end broken marriages without the statutory waiting period.

But the power has a limit. In Supreme Court Bar Association (1998) the Court held that Article 142 cannot override an express provision of a statute. So the power can fill gaps in the law, but cannot go against it.

cl.name: Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India
cl.facts: The Bhopal gas disaster settlement of $470 million, approved by the Court, was challenged — including the part quashing criminal proceedings against the company.
cl.held: The settlement was upheld under Article 142, but the quashing of criminal prosecutions was set aside. Article 142 cannot be used to override express statutory provisions, though it may supplement them.
cl.why: The first clear statement of the outer limit of the complete-justice power.

cl.name: Supreme Court Bar Association v. Union of India
cl.facts: In an earlier contempt case the Court had suspended an advocate's licence to practise — a power that belongs by statute to the Bar Council.
cl.held: Article 142 cannot be used to take over a jurisdiction that a statute vests in another body. The power is to do complete justice between parties in a cause before the Court, not to supplant the statutory scheme.
cl.why: Together with Union Carbide, it defines what Article 142 may not do — a boundary the Court has been reminded of repeatedly since.

sections.t: Power of the President to consult the Supreme Court
sections.b: (1) If at any time it appears to the President that a question of law or fact has arisen, or is likely to arise, which is of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the opinion of the Supreme Court upon it, he may refer the question to that Court for consideration and the Court may, after such hearing as it thinks fit, report to the President its opinion thereon. (2) The President may, notwithstanding anything in 2*** the proviso to article 131, refer a dispute of the kind mentioned in the 3[said proviso] to the Supreme Court for opinion and the Supreme Court shall, after such hearing as it thinks fit, report to the President its opinion thereon.
sections.cm:
The President may ask the Supreme Court for its opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance, whether it has arisen or is likely to arise. The Court may give its opinion.

For disputes arising from treaties made before the Constitution, which Article 131 excludes, the Court must give its opinion.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
On an ordinary reference the Court "may" answer, so it can refuse. The Court refused the Ayodhya reference of 1993.

An opinion is advice, not a judgment, and binds nobody, not even the President who asked. But in practice courts and governments follow it.

cl.name: In Re: Special Reference No. 1 of 1993, answered in Dr. M. Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India
cl.facts: After the Babri Masjid demolition, the President referred to the Court, on 7 January 1993, the question whether a Hindu temple had existed at the disputed site before the mosque was built. The Court answered the reference on 24 October 1994.
cl.held: The Court declined to answer. The question was superfluous, opposed to secularism, and favoured one religious community over another — and answering it would not serve any constitutional purpose.
cl.why: The clearest demonstration that 'may report' in Article 143(1) means the Court can refuse a reference outright.

sections.t: Civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court
sections.b: All authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.
sections.cm:
All authorities in India, civil and judicial, shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
There is no matching article for the High Courts. They rely instead on their power of superintendence under Article 227, and on their power to punish contempt.

sections.t: Special provisions as to disposal of questions relating to constitutional validity of laws
sections.b: Omitted.
sections.cm:
Article 144A required at least seven judges, and a two-thirds majority, to strike down a law as unconstitutional.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 42nd Amendment inserted it, and the 43rd repealed it in 1977.

sections.t: Rules of Court, etc
sections.b:
(1) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the Supreme Court may from time to time, with the approval of the President, make rules for regulating generally the practice and procedure of the Court including— (a) rules as to the persons practising before the Court; Amendment) (b) rules as to the procedure for hearing appeals and other matters pertaining to appeals including the time within which appeals to the Court are to be entered; (c) rules as to the proceedings in the Court for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III; 1[(cc) rules as to the proceedings in the Court under 2[article 139A];] (d) rules as to the entertainment of appeals under sub-clause (c) of clause (1) of article 134; (e) rules as to the conditions subject to which any judgment pronounced or order made by the Court may be reviewed and the procedure for such review including the time within which applications to the Court for such review are to be entered; (f) rules as to the costs of and incidental to any proceedings in the Court and as to the fees to be charged in respect of proceedings therein; (g) rules as to the granting of bail; (h) rules as to stay of proceedings; (i) rules providing for the summary determination of any appeal which appears to the Court to be frivolous or vexatious or brought for the purpose of delay; (j) rules as to the procedure for inquiries referred to in clause (1) of article 317. (2) Subject to the 3[provisions of 4*** clause (3)], rules made under this article may fix the minimum number of Judges who are to sit for any purpose, and may provide for the powers of single Judges and Division Courts. (3) 5[4***The minimum number] of Judges who are to sit for the purpose of deciding any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution or for the purpose of hearing any reference under article 143 shall be five: and 139A" of clause (3)" (4) No judgment shall be delivered by the Supreme Court save in open Court, and no report shall be made under article 143 save in accordance with an opinion also delivered in open Court. (5) No judgment and no such opinion shall be delivered by the Supreme Court save with the concurrence of a majority of the Judges present at the hearing of the case, but nothing in this clause shall be deemed to prevent a Judge who does not concur from delivering a dissenting judgment or opinion.

[Editorial Notes: 1. See the Supreme Court (Decrees and Orders) Enforcement Order, 1954 (C.O. 47). 2. The words, brackets and figure "clause (i) of" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh 3. Subs. by s. 29 and Sch., ibid., for "said clause" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956). 4. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 25 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977). 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 26 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977). 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 6, for "articles 131A 3. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 26, for "provisions 5. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 26, for "The 4. Certain words omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 6 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978). minimum number" (w.e.f. 1-2-1977). Provided that, where the Court hearing an appeal under any of the provisions of this Chapter other than article 132 consists of less than five Judges and in the course of the hearing of the appeal the Court is satisfied that the appeal involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the appeal, such Court shall refer the question for opinion to a Court constituted as required by this clause for the purpose of deciding any case involving such a question and shall on receipt of the opinion dispose of the appeal in conformity with such opinion.]
sections.cm:
The Supreme Court makes rules for its own practice and procedure, with the President's approval.

At least five judges must sit on a case that raises a substantial question about the meaning of the Constitution, or on a reference under Article 143. Judgments are given in open court, and judges may record dissents.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The five-judge minimum is where the term "Constitution Bench" comes from. Five is a floor, not a ceiling, which is how Kesavananda Bharati came to be heard by thirteen judges.

sections.t: Officers and servants and the expenses of the Supreme Court
sections.b: (1) Appointments of officers and servants of the Supreme Court shall be made by the Chief Justice of India or such other Judge or officer of the Court as he may direct: Provided that the President may by rule require that in such cases as may be specified in the rule, no person not already attached to the Court shall be appointed to any office connected with the Court, save after consultation with the Union Public Service Commission. (2) Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the conditions of service of officers and servants of the Supreme Court shall be such as may be prescribed by rules made by the Chief Justice of India or by some other Judge or officer of the Court authorised by the Chief Justice of India to make rules for the purpose: Provided that the rules made under this clause shall, so far as they relate to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions, require the approval of the President. (3) The administrative expenses of the Supreme Court, including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of the officers and servants of the Court, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India, and any fees or other moneys taken by the Court shall form part of that Fund.
sections.cm:
The Chief Justice appoints the officers and staff of the Supreme Court, and sets their conditions of service by rules. The Court's running costs are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Control over its own staff and money is the third support of judicial independence, alongside secure tenure and protected salaries.

sections.t: Interpretation
sections.b: In this Chapter and in Chapter V of Part VI, references to any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution shall be construed as including references to any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Government of India Act, 1935 (including any enactment amending or supplementing that Act), or of any Order in Council or order made thereunder, or of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, or of any order made thereunder.
sections.cm:
In this Chapter, questions about the meaning of the Constitution include questions about the Government of India Act, 1935, and the Indian Independence Act, 1947, and any law amending them.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
So arguments about which legislature can make a law still cite the Federal Court's decisions on the 1935 Act. Under Article 147 those are cases on the meaning of the Constitution.

sections.t: Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
sections.ct: THE UNION - COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL OF INDIA
sections.b: (1) There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India who shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and shall only be removed from office in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court. (2) Every person appointed to be the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India shall, before he enters upon his office, make and subscribe before the President, or some person appointed in that behalf by him, an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule. (3) The salary and other conditions of service of the Comptroller and Auditor-General shall be such as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until they are so determined, shall be as specified in the Second Schedule: Provided that neither the salary of a Comptroller and Auditor-General nor his rights in respect of leave of absence, pension or age of retirement shall be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment. (4) The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall not be eligible for further office either under the Government of India or under the Government of any State after he has ceased to hold his office. (5) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and of any law made by Parliament, the conditions of service of persons serving in the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and the administrative powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General shall be such as may be prescribed by rules made by the President after consultation with the Comptroller and Auditor-General. (6) The administrative expenses of the office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General, including all salaries, allowances and pensions payable to or in respect of persons serving in that office, shall be charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
sections.cm:
There shall be a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, appointed by the President by warrant.

The CAG can be removed only in the way, and on the grounds, that a Supreme Court judge can be. The office's expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 148 fixes no term. The six years, or age 65 if earlier, come from a 1971 Act of Parliament. What the article guarantees is that the terms cannot be changed for the worse after appointment.

After leaving office, the CAG cannot hold any other office under the Union or a State. The bar removes any reason to soften an audit in the hope of a later job.

cl.name: Association of Unified Telecom Service Providers v. Union of India
cl.facts: Private telecom operators resisted a CAG audit of their revenue accounts, arguing the CAG audits government, not private companies.
cl.held: Where a private party shares revenue with the government under a licence, the CAG may audit its accounts. Article 149 read with the CAG Act extends to any body whose receipts affect the Consolidated Fund.
cl.why: It extended constitutional audit into public-private revenue-sharing arrangements — spectrum, mining, highways.

sections.t: Duties and powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General
sections.ct: THE UNION - COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL OF INDIA
sections.b: The Comptroller and Auditor-General shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States and of any other authority or body as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament and, until provision in that behalf is so made, shall perform such duties and exercise such powers in relation to the accounts of the Union and of the States as were conferred on or exercisable by the Auditor-General of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution in relation to the accounts of the Dominion of India and of the Provinces respectively.
sections.cm:
The CAG performs the duties and uses the powers that Parliament lays down by law, for the accounts of the Union, the States and other bodies.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The substance is in an ordinary law, the Comptroller and Auditor-General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, not in the Constitution.

So Parliament decides how far the CAG's audit reaches, and can change it by an ordinary law.

sections.t: Form of accounts of the Union and of the States
sections.ct: THE UNION - COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL OF INDIA
sections.b: The accounts of the Union and of the States shall be kept in such form as the President may, 2[on the advice of] the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, prescribe.]
sections.cm:
The accounts of the Union and the States are kept in the form the President prescribes, on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 44th Amendment changed the words "after consultation with" to "on the advice of". The change gave the CAG more say over how the accounts are kept.

sections.t: Audit reports
sections.ct: THE UNION - COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL OF INDIA
sections.b:
(1) The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India relating to the accounts of the Union shall be submitted to the President, who shall cause them to be laid before each House of Parliament. (2) The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India relatingto the accounts of a State shall besubmitted to the Governor 3*** of the State, who shall cause them to be laid before the Legislature of the State.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 27, for art.150 2. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 22, for "after 3. The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment)]
sections.cm:
The CAG's reports on the Union's accounts go to the President, who has them laid before both Houses. Reports on a State's accounts go to the Governor, who has them laid before the State legislature.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The report is only laid. The Constitution creates no duty to act on it.

The follow-up happens in the Public Accounts Committee, which the rules of Parliament create, not Article 151.

sections.t: Definition
sections.b: In this Part, unless the context otherwise requires, the expression “State” 2[does not include the State of Jammu and Kashmir].
sections.cm:
In Part VI, "State" does not include Jammu and Kashmir.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The exclusion no longer matters. Since the 2019 reorganisation, Jammu and Kashmir is a Union territory, governed under Part VIII.

sections.t: Governors of States
sections.b: There shall be a Governor for each State: 3[Provided that nothing in this article shall prevent the appointment of the same person as Governor for two or more States.]
sections.cm:
Every State has a Governor. One person may be Governor of two or more States.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 7th Amendment (1956) allowed one person to be Governor of two or more States. Shared Governors are now common, especially in the north-east. So the Constitution does not insist on a separate Governor for every State.

sections.t: Executive power of State
sections.b: (1) The executive power of the State shall be vested in the Governor and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution. (2) Nothing in this article shall— (a) be deemed to transfer to the Governor any functions conferred by any existing law on any other authority; or (b) prevent Parliament or the Legislature of the State from conferring by law functions on any authority subordinate to the Governor.
sections.cm:
The executive power of the State is vested in the Governor. The Governor uses it directly or through officers below the Governor.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 154 mirrors Article 53, and like it, the vesting is a formality. The substance is in Article 163.

sections.t: Appointment of Governor
sections.b: The Governor of a State shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
sections.cm:
The President appoints the Governor of a State by warrant under the President's hand and seal.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Governor is appointed, not elected, and that is the biggest difference from the Union model. The draft Constitution had an elected Governor. The Constituent Assembly dropped it, because two elected heads in one State would clash.

Nothing in the text requires the Union to consult the State government first. Consulting the Chief Minister is only a convention, and it has often been ignored.

sections.t: Term of office of Governor
sections.b:
(1) The Governor shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. (2) The Governor may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office. (3) Subject to the foregoing provisions of this article, a Governor shall hold office for a term of five years from the date on which he enters upon his office: (Seventh Amendment) Schedule" Provided that a Governor shall, notwithstanding the expiration of his term, continue to hold office until his successor enters upon his office.

[Editorial Notes: 1. The words "IN PART A OF THE FIRST SCHEDULE" omitted by the Constitution 2. Subs. by s. 29 and Sch. ibid., for "means a State specified in Part A of the First 3. Added by s. 6, ibid. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).]
sections.cm:
The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President, for a term of five years. A Governor may resign to the President, and stays in office until a successor takes over.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
"During the pleasure" overrides the five-year term. The President acts on the Union government's advice, so the Union can remove a Governor at any time.

B.P. Singhal (2010) put a limit on the power. Removal cannot be arbitrary, or based only on a change of government at the centre. But no reasons need be given and no hearing is required, so the limit is hard to enforce.

sections.t: Qualifications for appointment as Governor
sections.b: No person shall be eligible for appointment as Governor unless he is a citizen of India and has completed the age of thirty-five years.
sections.cm:
A Governor must be a citizen of India and at least thirty-five years old.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Constitution sets only those two conditions. There is no requirement of neutrality, no bar on past party office, and no duty to consult the State.

The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions both recommended more conditions. None were added.

sections.t: Conditions of Governor's office
sections.b: (1) The Governor shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any State specified in the First Schedule, and if a member of either House of Parliament or of a House of the Legislature of any such State be appointed Governor, he shall be deemed to have vacated his seat in that House on the date on which he enters upon his office as Governor. (2) The Governor shall not hold any other office of profit. (3) The Governor shall be entitled without payment of rent to the use of his official residences and shall be also entitled to such emoluments, allowances and privileges as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until provision in that behalf is so made, such emoluments, allowances and privileges as are specified in the Second Schedule. 1[(3A) Where the same person is appointed as Governor of two or more States, the emoluments and allowances payable to the Governor shall be allocated among the States in such proportion as the President may by order determine.] (4) The emoluments and allowances of the Governor shall not be diminished during his term of office.
sections.cm:
A Governor cannot be a member of a legislature or hold any other office of profit. The Governor gets a rent-free residence and the pay set out in the Second Schedule, which cannot be cut during the term.

Where one person is Governor of two States, the pay is shared between them as the President directs.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The bar on cutting the pay protects little in practice. Under Article 156 a Governor holds office at the President's pleasure, so a Governor who displeases the Union can simply be removed.

sections.t: Oath or affirmation by the Governor
sections.b:
Every Governor and every person discharging the functions of the Governor shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe in the presence of the Chief Justice of the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to the State, or, in his absence, the senior most Judge of that Court available, an oath or affirmation in the following form, that is to say— “I, A. B., do swear in the name of God that I will faithfully execute the solemnly affirm office of Governor (or discharge the functions of the Governor) of . ...... (name of the State) and will to the best of my ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law and that I will devote myself to the service and well-being of the people of ........ (name of the State).”.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Ins. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 7 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).]
sections.cm:
The Governor takes the oath before the Chief Justice of the High Court. The Governor swears to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and to serve the people of the State.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The oath is to the people of the State. But the Union appoints and removes the Governor, and the two do not sit easily together.

sections.t: Discharge of the functions of the Governor in certain contingencies
sections.b: The President may make such provision as he thinks fit for the discharge of the functions of the Governor of a State in any contingency not provided for in this Chapter.
sections.cm:
The President may provide for the Governor's functions to be carried out in any situation this Chapter does not cover.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The power is used when a Governor dies or resigns suddenly. The President usually asks the Governor of a neighbouring State, or the Chief Justice of the High Court, to take charge for a while.

sections.t: Power of Governor to grant pardons, etc., and to suspend, remit or commute sentences in certain cases
sections.b: The Governor of a State shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
sections.cm:
The Governor may pardon a convict, or suspend, remit or commute a sentence, for offences against laws on matters within the State's executive power.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Governor's power differs from the President's in two ways. The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence, though the Governor can commute it to life imprisonment. And the Governor has no power over court-martial sentences.

Like the President, the Governor acts on the advice of ministers, as Maru Ram (1980) settled. Courts review the decision only on narrow grounds.

sections.t: Extent of executive power of State
sections.b: Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, the executive power of a State shall extend to the matters with respect to which the Legislature of the State has power to make laws: Provided that in any matter with respect to which the Legislature of a State and Parliament have power to make laws, the executive power of the State shall be subject to, and limited by, the executive power expressly conferred by this Constitution or by any law made by Parliament upon the Union or authorities thereof.
sections.cm:
The executive power of a State covers the matters on which its legislature can make laws.

On a subject where both Parliament and the State can make laws, the State's executive power gives way to any executive power the Constitution or a law of Parliament expressly gives the Union.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 162 mirrors Article 73. But the Union gains executive power on a Concurrent subject only where its law says so expressly. Making a law on the subject is not enough by itself.

sections.t: Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor
sections.b: (1) There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion. (2) If any question arises whether any matter is or is not a matter as respects which the Governor is by or under this Constitution required to act in his discretion, the decision of the Governor in his discretion shall be final, and the validity of anything done by the Governor shall not be called in question on the ground that he ought or ought not to have acted in his discretion. (3) The question whether any, and if so what, advice was tendered by Ministers to the Governor shall not be inquired into in any court.
sections.cm:
A Council of Ministers, led by the Chief Minister, aids and advises the Governor. The exception is where the Constitution requires the Governor to act in the Governor's discretion.

If a question arises whether a matter is within that discretion, the Governor's decision is final. No court may ask what advice the ministers gave.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 74 has no such exception for the President. So the Governor has real personal power that the President lacks, and the office is fought over for that reason.

Some discretion is written into the text, such as reserving a Bill for the President under Article 200. Some arises from events, such as choosing a Chief Minister when no party has a majority.

But the courts have narrowed it. Shamsher Singh (1974) held that acting on advice is the rule and discretion the exception. Nabam Rebia (2016) held that the Governor's discretion is open to judicial review.

cl.name: Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly
cl.facts: The Arunachal Pradesh Governor advanced the Assembly session by a month and fixed its agenda on his own, while a motion to remove the Speaker was pending. A rival government was sworn in.
cl.held: The Governor's discretion under Article 163 is not unlimited and is subject to judicial review. He cannot summon, prorogue or set the agenda of the House on his own — those are functions to be performed on ministerial advice. The status quo ante was restored.
cl.why: The first time a dismissed State government was reinstated by court order, and the clearest limit yet placed on gubernatorial discretion.

sections.t: Other provisions as to Ministers
sections.b:
(1) The Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor and the other Ministers shall be appointed by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister, and the Ministers shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor: Provided that in the States of 1[Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand], Madhya Pradesh and 2[Odisha] there shall be a Minister in charge of tribal welfare who may in addition be in charge of the welfare of the Scheduled Castes and backward classes or any other work. 3[(1A) The total number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, in the Council of Ministers in a State shall not exceed fifteen per cent. of the total number of members of the Legislative Assembly of that State: Provided that the number of Ministers, including the Chief Minister in a State shall not be less than twelve: Provided further that where the total number of Ministers including the Chief Minister in the Council of Ministers in any State at the commencement of the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003 exceeds the said fifteen per cent. or the number specified in the first proviso, as the case may be, then the total number of Ministers in that State shall be brought in conformity with the provisions of this clause within six months from such date4 as the President may by public notification appoint. (1B) A member of the Legislative Assembly of a State or either House of the Legislature of a State having Legislative Council belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of that House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified to be appointed as a Minister under clause (1) for duration of the period commencing from the date of his disqualification till the date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or where he contests any election to the Legislative Assembly of a State or either House of the Legislature of a State having Legislative Council, as the case may be, before the expiry of such period, till the date on which he is declared elected, whichever is earlier.] (2) The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State. (3) Before a Minister enters upon his office, the Governor shall administer to him the oaths of office and of secrecy according to the forms set out for the purpose in the Third Schedule. 4. 7-1-2004, vide notification number S.O. 21(E), dated 7-1-2004. (4) A Minister who for any period of six consecutive months is not a member of the Legislature of the State shall at the expiration of that period cease to be a Minister. (5) The salaries and allowances of Ministers shall be such as the Legislature of the State may from time to time by law determine and, until the Legislature of the State so determines, shall be as specified in the Second Schedule.

[Editorial Notes: 1. Subs. by the Constitution (Ninety-fourth Amendment) Act, 2006, s. 2, for "Bihar" 2. Subs. by the Orissa (Alteration of Name) Act, 2011 (15 of 2011), s. 4, for "Orissa" 3. Ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 3 (w.e.f. 1-1-2004).]
sections.cm:
The Governor appoints the Chief Minister, and appoints the other ministers on the Chief Minister's advice. Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure.

The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly. A minister who is not a member of the legislature must become one within six months.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The 91st Amendment (2003) added clause (1A). A State ministry may have no more than 15 per cent of the Assembly's strength, and no fewer than twelve ministers. The Union cap has no such floor.

The floor keeps the ministry workable where 15 per cent of the Assembly would be too few.

sections.t: Advocate-General for the State
sections.b: (1) The Governor of each State shall appoint a person who is qualified to be appointed a Judge of a High Court to be Advocate-General for the State. (2) It shall be the duty of the Advocate-General to give advice to the Government of the State upon such legal matters, and to perform such other duties of a legal character, as may from time to time be referred or assigned to him by the Governor, and to discharge the functions conferred on him by or under this Constitution or any other law for the time being in force. (3) The Advocate-General shall hold office during the pleasure of the Governor, and shall receive such remuneration as the Governor may determine.
sections.cm:
The Governor appoints an Advocate-General for the State, who must be qualified to be a High Court judge. The Advocate-General advises the State government on legal matters and carries out the legal duties assigned.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The Advocate-General is the State's version of the Attorney-General. Under Article 177 the Advocate-General may speak in the State legislature, but cannot vote.

sections.t: Conduct of Business of the Government of a State
sections.b: (1) All executive action of the Government of a State shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the Governor. (2) Orders and other instruments made and executed in the name of the Governor shall be authenticated in such manner as may be specified in rules to be made by the Governor, and the validity of an order or instrument which is so authenticated shall not be called in question on the ground that it is not an order or instrument made or executed by the Governor. (3) The Governor shall make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of the State, and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business in so far as it is not business with respect to which the Governor is by or under this Constitution required to act in his discretion. 1(4)* * * * *
sections.cm:
All executive action of a State is taken in the Governor's name. An order signed in the prescribed way cannot be challenged on the ground that the Governor did not make it.

The Governor makes rules for conducting the government's business and dividing it among the ministers.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
The signing rule protects an order only from challenges to its form, and does not cure a lack of power. An order made by someone with no power to make it is still void.

sections.t: Duties of Chief Minister as respects the furnishing of information to Governor, etc
sections.b: It shall be the duty of the Chief Minister of each State— (a) to communicate to the Governor of the State all decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation; (b) to furnish such information relating to the administration of the affairs of the State and proposals for legislation as the Governor may call for; and (c) if the Governor so requires, to submit for the consideration of the Council of Ministers any matter on which a decision has been taken by a Minister but which has not been considered by the Council.
sections.cm:
The Chief Minister has three duties towards the Governor.

The Chief Minister must report all decisions of the Council of Ministers on administration and legislation. The Chief Minister must give any information on those matters that the Governor asks for. And if the Governor asks, the Chief Minister must put a decision taken by one minister alone before the whole Council.

Judicial Nuance & Exceptions:
Article 167 is the Governor's main channel for learning what the State government is doing. The information also feeds the Governor's report to the President under Article 356. So disputes often start when a Governor asks a State government for files.

But the duty is to inform, not to obey. The Governor can make the whole Council look at a decision again, but cannot make it change the decision.

sections.t: Constitution of Legislatures in States
sections.b:
(1) For every State there shall be a Legislature which shall consist of the Governor, and— (a) in the States of 2*** 3[Andhra Pradesh], Bihar, 4*** 5[Madhya Pradesh], 6*** 7[Maharashtra], 8[Karnataka], 9*** and (2) Where there are two Houses of the Legislature of a State, one shall be known as the Legislative Council and the other as the Legislative Assembly, and where there is only one House, it shall be known as the Legislative Assembly.
